user_input.one_line: Records the human's real keyboard and mouse, system-wide, into the active profile's JSONL — the only emitter that can show input the program never handled. Privacy-sensitive: never a default.
user_input.what_it_does: A SEPARATE long-running process (python_backend/daemon/input_daemon.py) taps the OS input layer and appends unified-schema JSONL records to the ACTIVE profile's action_log_file. Nothing is loaded into the target program. Per OS: macOS uses a Quartz CGEventTap (kCGHIDEventTap, listen-only) and calls an event PHYSICAL when kCGEventSourceUnixProcessID == 0; Windows installs WH_KEYBOARD_LL + WH_MOUSE_LL global hooks and calls an event physical when the injected flag (LLKHF_INJECTED 0x10 / LLMHF_INJECTED 0x01) is NOT set; Linux reads /dev/input/event* with evdev and classifies PER DEVICE (a uinput/virtual device — sysfs under /devices/virtual/, empty `phys` — is synthetic, real HID is physical). Synthetic (bot-injected) events are recorded whenever the daemon runs. PHYSICAL events — the human's own typing and clicking — are DROPPED unless the active profile has capture_user_input = true. That flag is what this emitter turns on. It is system-wide: there is no window, app, or process filter anywhere in the daemon, so it records keystrokes typed into every other application too.
captures: Physical key press and release: source av.daemon.key.press / av.daemon.key.release, category "key", data.keycode, data.phase (down|up), data.kind = "physical", data.source_pid = 0.
Physical mouse clicks: av.daemon.mouse.click with data.button (left|right|middle|x1|x2), data.phase (down|up), and screen coords in both data.x/data.y and the record's coords field.
Scroll: av.daemon.mouse.scroll with data.dx / data.dy plus coords.
Mouse movement, coalesced to at most one record per 100 ms (COALESCE_MS), carrying the LATEST position and the hardware timestamp of that move (not of the flush tick).

macOS extra: modifier-key changes as av.daemon.key.modifier, data.phase = "flags". Windows extra: data.scancode. Linux extra: data.repeat = true for OS autorepeat, and data.device = the evdev device name.

Hardware event time: ts_ms comes from the OS event clock anchored to wall clock (mach_absolute_time on macOS, GetTickCount on Windows, ev.timestamp() on Linux). ts_recv_ms is when the daemon received it, so kernel-to-userland lag is measurable.
Daemon lifecycle: av.daemon.start (carries pid, os, active_profile, active_sink, capture_user_input), av.daemon.exit on signal, and av.daemon.selftest on Windows/Linux.

Also, with no flag and no selection needed: SYNTHETIC input injected by a bot (pyautogui / SendInput / cliclick / CGEventPost / ydotool) is recorded whenever the daemon runs, marked data.kind = "synthetic" (data.source_pid = the real injector pid on macOS, -1 on Windows/Linux).
misses: WHICH WINDOW OR APP received the input. There is no focus or window field in any record. A key typed into your program and a key typed into a chat app look identical.
Characters and text. Only raw OS keycodes (Windows vkCode + scanCode, macOS CGKeyCode, Linux evdev code). No keyboard-layout translation, no assembled strings, no clipboard.

What the program DID with the input. The daemon is outside the process: it proves a key reached the OS, and says nothing about handlers, dispatch, or whether the program ever read it. That half needs an in-process emitter.
Fast pointer paths. Moves are subsampled to ~10 per second, so the intermediate path of a drag or a flick is lost. Keys, clicks and scroll are recorded event-for-event.
frame_seq. The daemon writes frame_seq: null in every record, so screenshot correlation is by TIMESTAMP only (av_actions_around_frame windows on ts_ms) — never by sequence number.
Touch, pen and gamepad buttons. Linux quirk from the code: any device reporting ABS_X/ABS_Y (touchpad, tablet, joystick) is folded into the pointer position, so those coordinates can be wrong.
Everything while the daemon process is not running, and everything while a DIFFERENT profile is active: the sink follows active_profile.txt, so records can land in another project's actions.jsonl.

Linux: injection that bypasses /dev/input — X11 XTEST (xdotool's default) or Wayland virtual-pointer protocols — is invisible. Physical mouse coordinates there are accumulated from relative deltas anchored best-effort (xdotool on X11, else 0,0).
macOS: there is no --selftest for this backend; the CLI self-test returns ok = null on macOS, so "it is armed" must be verified from the records, not from a self-test.
user_input.lang_reason: It is an out-of-process OS tap, not an in-process hook. Nothing is imported, preloaded, or linked into the target, so the target's language is irrelevant — a compiled C binary, a browser page, a Go service, a shell script and a Python script are all recorded identically. The language constraint is on the HOST, not the target: the daemon is Python and needs pyobjc-framework-Quartz on macOS (exit 2 without it) or python-evdev on Linux (exit 2 without it).
use_when: The target reads keys directly and logs nothing about them: msvcrt.getch, curses getch/getkey, tty.setraw + termios, readchar, keyboard.on_press, pynput.keyboard.Listener.
The target has an event loop that consumes input: pygame.event.get with KEYDOWN, SDL_PollEvent, glfwSetKeyCallback, Qt keyPressEvent, tkinter bind("<Key..."), an on_key_press callback.
The complaint is "it ignores my key" or "my click does nothing". You need proof the input existed at all before blaming the handler.
You need input-to-reaction latency: this emitter timestamps the key at the hardware, the target's own emitter timestamps the reaction.
A HUMAN is reproducing the bug by hand, or demonstrating a workflow to be replayed later (RPA recording). For that run the human is the agent.
visual_capture is true and the frames change for reasons no log explains — the missing cause is usually a click or a keystroke.
The user has explicitly agreed, in this session, to their own keyboard and mouse being recorded.
do_not_use_when: The user has not explicitly agreed. This records the human's real keystrokes system-wide, including anything typed into other applications. Never select it as a default and never to "be thorough".

Headless service, REST backend, CI job, container, cron task, data pipeline, library test suite — nobody is at a keyboard, and on Windows the low-level hooks need an interactive desktop session at all.
The run is driven by an automation script and you only want the script's actions. Synthetic events are already recorded by the daemon alone; this flag adds only the human's input on top.
The failure is in code that never touches input (parser, migration, request handler, file walker). The records add volume and dilute every av_log_* and digest read of the same file.
You need to know which widget or window received the key. It cannot tell you; that needs an in-process or UI-level hook.
Long unattended sessions: about 10 mouse-move records per second while the pointer moves, plus 2 records per keystroke, into the same JSONL every other tool reads.
The machine is shared, being screen-shared, or in use by someone other than the person who agreed.
user_input.cost: One extra long-running process, outside the target. Volume: 2 records per keystroke and up to ~10 mouse-move records per second while the pointer moves, appended to the profile's actions.jsonl that every other AgentVision tool reads. macOS: one-time Accessibility grant (CGEventTapCreate fails, exit 3, without it) plus pyobjc-framework-Quartz. Linux: python-evdev plus read access to /dev/input/event* (input group; exit 3 with the group hint otherwise). Windows: no special permission, but the hook callbacks only ENQUEUE (a worker thread does the JSON write) because a callback slower than LowLevelHooksTimeout makes Windows silently drop the hook; the daemon re-probes with a SendInput VK_F24 handshake every AGENTVISION_HOOK_REVERIFY_S (default 120 s) and reinstalls on the owner thread. The real cost is privacy: the human's keystrokes end up in the project's log file.
user_input.builds_as: NOTHING is written into the target project, and the target is not restarted. Two parts must both exist: (1) capture_user_input = true on the ACTIVE profile (a ProgramProfile field persisted in python_backend/profiles.json); (2) the daemon process python_backend/daemon/input_daemon.py, started detached by `agentvision daemon start`, by `agentvision run --record-input` (or AGENTVISION_RECORD_INPUT=1), or by the GUI Permissions tab. Records append to the active profile's action_log_file, which for a bridged project the installer already points at <project>/agentvision/actions.jsonl. The daemon re-reads the profile flag every 2 s (PROFILE_REFRESH_S), so flipping it takes effect without restarting the daemon or the program.
user_input.enforced: Gated at runtime — but by the DAEMON, not by AGENTVISION_HOOKS. The gate is _gate() in input_daemon.py: it re-reads the active profile's capture_user_input every 2 s and DROPS every physical event while it is false, counting them in dropped_physical. Two conditions must both hold or nothing physical is recorded: the daemon is running AND the flag is true. Be exact about the second half: as of today no bridge-commit or installer path sets that flag — only the GUI Permissions tab and POST /profiles write it, and `agentvision run --record-input` starts the daemon WITHOUT setting it. So unless the commit wiring also sets capture_user_input, selecting this id is recorded intent, not an armed capture. The synthetic half is not gated at all: with the daemon running, injected events are recorded whatever the plan says.
user_input.how_to_verify: 1) av_daemon_status() returns running: true, capture_user_input: true, and active_sink pointing at this project's actions.jsonl. 2) The sink contains a record with source "av.daemon.start" whose data.capture_user_input is true. 3) Press one key, then av_search / av_log_range the sink for source "av.daemon.key.press" with data.kind == "physical" and data.source_pid == 0 — if every record's kind is "synthetic", the flag is off. 4) The daemon's own log (agentvision_daemon.log in the OS temp dir) prints "target -> profile=... capture_user_input=True" on change and a stats line every 30 s; dropped_physical rising while you type means the flag is off. 5) av_preflight's input_daemon check reports ok: false when the profile asks for capture and the daemon is dead.
benefit_examples: A 60-line Python keypress utility (curses getch loop, prints nothing). Complaint: "the arrow keys do nothing." The sink shows av.daemon.key.press keycode=126 phase=down kind=physical at 12:00:03.412, and the program's own records show nothing within 500 ms — the key reached the OS and the loop never handled it. With no input emitter the run is silent on both sides, and a dead handler is indistinguishable from a key that was never pressed.

A pygame game loop that eats jumps under load. Key down at t, key up at t+95 ms, and the program's next frame record at t+380 ms: the whole press fell inside one long frame. The in-process hooks only ever see the events the loop actually processed, so a dropped press is invisible to them by construction.

A browser SPA whose tab freezes "while typing in the search box". av_browser.js records errors, console output and failed fetches — it records no keyboard events at all. This emitter supplies the keystroke times: 9 presses in 1.2 s, then the last console record 3 s later, so the freeze starts on a specific keystroke rather than at page load. It cannot say which input element received them.

A tkinter/PyQt desktop GUI bug that only reproduces when a human clicks fast. The records give the exact gesture: down/up at (412,208), then a second down/up 90 ms later — a replayable sequence, alignable to the frame timeline by ts_ms. Screenshots show the broken result; only this emitter shows the gesture that caused it. The same mechanism turns a human demonstrating an RPA workflow into a recorded action list.
code_signals: Raw key reads: msvcrt.getch, curses, getch(, tty.setraw, termios, readchar, keyboard.on_press, keyboard.wait, pynput
Input-consuming event loops: pygame.event.get, KEYDOWN, KEYUP, SDL_PollEvent, glfwSetKeyCallback, keyPressEvent, bind("<Key, addEventListener('keydown'

Injectors — the program DRIVES input (argues for running the daemon at all; the synthetic half needs no flag): pyautogui, pydirectinput, SendInput, cliclick, CGEventPost, ydotool, uinput, robotjs, AppleScript keystroke
A gui_toolkit signal in catalog.code_evidence (tkinter|PyQt|PySide|kivy|SDL|GLFW|imgui|electron) together with visual_capture: true
Absence is decisive: no key or mouse read and no injector anywhere in the target means do not select this.
user_input.caveat: PRIVACY. This is the only emitter that records the HUMAN, not the program, and it is system-wide with no per-window or per-app filter — keystrokes typed into a password manager, a browser, or a chat app land in the project's actions.jsonl as raw keycodes, which are trivially reversible to text. It must never be selected by default, never bundled into an "install everything" plan, and never enabled without the user saying yes in this session. It also runs independently of the target's lifetime, so it keeps recording between runs and while the target is closed. Second-order trap: the daemon writes to whatever profile active_profile.txt names, so a wrong active profile silently sends one project's human input into another project's log.

lifecycle.one_line: Two records per run: the program started (pid, argv, cwd) and the program ended. Nothing in between.
lifecycle.what_it_does: Marks the boundaries of a run in <project>/agentvision/actions.jsonl. On Python, agent_bootstrap/av_runtime.py install_all_hooks() writes one `process` record named av.bootstrap.start inline at import, and registers an atexit handler that writes av.bootstrap.exit. On Node, agentvision/emitters/av_emit.js writes av.node.start at load and av.node.exit from process.on('exit'). On Ruby, av_emit.rb writes av.ruby.start and, from at_exit, av.ruby.exit. On every other language nothing is installed that does this; the only run boundary comes from the `agentvision run` wrapper (python_backend/cli.py cmd_run), which writes av.wrapper.start and av.wrapper.exit whatever the plan said. This emitter answers one question: did a run happen, with what arguments, and did it reach a clean exit.
captures: Python av.bootstrap.start (category `process`): pid, argv, python version, cwd, project root.

Python av.bootstrap.start also carries hooks_requested, hooks_armed, hooks_selection_source and catches_swallowed_exceptions. This is the ONLY place the agent can read which hooks actually armed instead of guessing from silence.
Python av.bootstrap.exit (category `process`) at atexit: pid ONLY. No exit code, no status, no duration.
Node av.node.start (pid, argv, node version, cwd) and av.node.exit (pid AND `code`). Node is the only language whose installed emitter reports the exit code.
Ruby av.ruby.start (pid, argv, ruby version, cwd) and av.ruby.exit (pid only).
run_id on every record (format av-<epoch_ms>-<pid>), which is how you separate this run from the previous run in the same append-only file.
frame_seq on Python records, read from <project>/agentvision/.av_frame_seq, so a run boundary is pinned to a screenshot number.

The same Python atexit handler flushes stdout/stderr and, if swallowed_exceptions also armed, writes av.bootstrap.swallowed_summary with the true per-site totals. The exit path is what delivers those totals.
When launched through `agentvision run`, cli.py additionally writes av.wrapper.start (run_id, argv, project, wrapper_pid) and av.wrapper.exit (run_id, exit_code) — independent of this selection.
misses: Everything between start and exit. No log lines, no function calls, no requests, no errors, no values.

The exit code, on Python and Ruby. The exit record contains only the pid. The catalog line that says lifecycle captures 'exit code' is wrong for those two languages. Only Node's av.node.exit carries `code`, and only the wrapper's av.wrapper.exit carries it for everything else.

Any death that skips atexit / at_exit: kill -9 (SIGKILL), os._exit(), a segfault inside a C extension, a hard power loss. You get a start record and NO exit record. Absence is the only evidence, and it looks identical to 'still running'.
The swallowed_exceptions summary is lost in the same way, because it rides on the same atexit handler.

Nothing at all on java, .NET, go, rust, c, c++, shell. The logback XML and the Serilog JSON only format the app's own logger calls; av_emit.go only defines Emit(); av_emit.sh only defines av_log. None of them run at process start or exit. On those languages the only lifecycle data is from `agentvision run`.
Duration. Neither record contains an elapsed time or the other record's timestamp. Subtract ts_ms yourself.
Child processes. A program that forks workers gets one start record, for the parent.
A hang. A frozen process emits the start record and then nothing — the same shape as a crash.

On Python launched via `agentvision run`, the wrapper's run_id and the in-process emitter's run_id are DIFFERENT values (cli.py reads AGENTVISION_RUN_ID; av_runtime._RUN_ID is built from its own time and pid and never reads that env var). One run therefore appears under two run_ids: av.wrapper.* under one, av.bootstrap.* under the other. Do not group a run by run_id alone.
languages: any other language ONLY through `agentvision run`
lifecycle.lang_reason: The record has to be written by code running inside the program at startup and at shutdown. That needs an interpreter injection point: Python's sitecustomize/PYTHONPATH plus atexit, Node's NODE_OPTIONS=--require plus process.on('exit'), Ruby's RUBYOPT=-r plus at_exit. A compiled binary has no interpreter startup to inject into, so there is nothing to hook without changing the build. The java/.NET artifacts are log-formatter configs, not process hooks, so they cannot see start or exit either. For all of those the process boundary is observable only from OUTSIDE, which is what run_wrapper does.
program_kinds: CLI batch job or cron task that is expected to finish
test runner or harness invoked hundreds of times
desktop GUI launched by the user by hand
game loop or long-run emulator where frames must be segmented per run
any program restarted repeatedly against the same actions.jsonl
short-lived script whose only current symptom is 'nothing happened'
use_when: The program is started repeatedly and actions.jsonl already holds records from several past runs, so runs need boundaries. Check with av_log_raw() for more than one run_id value.
Something else launches it: a crontab entry, a Makefile target, an npm script, a .sh launcher, a systemd unit, a docker command in the repo.
The code reads sys.argv / process.argv / ARGV / argparse and behaves differently per flag, so knowing which flags a given run used is diagnostic.
The program is designed to finish: a top-level main() with sys.exit(main()), no accept loop. Then 'did it finish' is a real, answerable question.
The user's report is 'it does nothing' or 'it does not open'. The start record is the cheapest possible proof of life and tells you whether the process was ever created.
visual_capture is true and screenshots must be attributed to runs — Python lifecycle records carry frame_seq.
You want ONLY lifecycle on Python, in order to switch the other four hooks off. Selecting lifecycle alone is how that is expressed (see `enforced`).
do_not_use_when: You need to know WHY a run failed. This carries no exception, no message, no traceback. Select uncaught_exceptions or stdout_tee for that.
The language is java, .NET, go, rust, c, c++ or shell and the program will not be launched through `agentvision run`. Then this selection produces zero records.

You already selected run_wrapper. The wrapper writes av.wrapper.start/exit and its exit record carries the exit code that Python's does not. The catalog states outright that selecting both is not additive.
The target is a long-lived daemon that starts once and never exits. You get one record at boot and silence forever; every interesting failure is in the middle.
A supervisor hard-kills the program by design (timeout, SIGKILL). The exit record will never appear, so do not build a 'did it finish' check on it.

You are choosing it on Python believing it is what produces the start record. It is not — see `enforced`. Pick it for the exclusion effect or for the honest reason, not for a record you would get anyway.
It is your only selection on a program with real failures to find. Two records per run is not a bridge; it is a heartbeat.
lifecycle.cost: Two JSONL records per run and one atexit handler. No per-line, per-call or per-exception overhead. Nothing measurable. On Python the start record is written whether or not lifecycle is selected, so choosing it costs literally nothing extra.
lifecycle.builds_as: No file of its own. On Python it is a facet of the sitecustomize.py + agent_bootstrap/av_runtime.py install (install_all_hooks emits av.bootstrap.start inline and calls atexit.register(_on_exit)). On Node it is the process.on('exit') block inside <project>/agentvision/emitters/av_emit.js. On Ruby it is the at_exit block inside av_emit.rb. On every other language nothing is built for it — the records come from python_backend/cli.py cmd_run.
lifecycle.enforced: MIXED — read carefully, do not simplify this. On Python the id does reach the runtime: installer.py bakes AGENTVISION_HOOKS into the generated sitecustomize.py and av_runtime._selected_hooks() reads it. BUT the two lifecycle records are emitted UNCONDITIONALLY. In install_all_hooks the `if "lifecycle" in _want` branch only appends the name to the reported hooks_armed list, and atexit.register(_on_exit) sits outside every gate. So not selecting lifecycle does not remove the records, and selecting it does not add them. What selecting it DOES do is act as a whitelist: AGENTVISION_HOOKS becomes exactly your list, so the four other hooks are switched OFF. Selecting nothing, or selecting all five, leaves AGENTVISION_HOOKS unset — and unset means arm EVERYTHING (emitters.hooks_env returns {} in both cases). On Node and Ruby: recorded as intent only. av_emit.js and av_emit.rb never read AGENTVISION_HOOKS; they always emit lifecycle plus the console tee plus the exception handlers. Note that emitters.selection_report() still reports enforced: true for lifecycle on node/ruby — that report is wrong for those two, and the EmitterSpec itself sets selection_enforced=False for them. On java, .NET, go, rust, c, c++, shell and unknown: recorded as intent, one artifact, and that artifact emits no lifecycle at all. Leak (2) is now DISCLOSED rather than silent: emitters.hooks_fail_open() returns the list of hooks that will arm anyway, and the install report carries it as emitter_selection_fail_open. Confirm against the av.bootstrap.start record's hooks_armed / hooks_selection_source, which is ground truth.
lifecycle.how_to_verify: 1) Launch through the wrapper: `agentvision run -- python your_script.py`. A plain `python your_script.py` emits nothing — CPython imports sitecustomize before the script's directory joins sys.path, measured on Homebrew python and a clean venv, and stated in <project>/agentvision/emitters/README.txt. 2) Read the sink: av_log_raw(), or grep av.bootstrap.start in <project>/agentvision/actions.jsonl. You want a record with category `process` and source `av.bootstrap.start`. 3) In that record read hooks_armed and hooks_requested — that is the authoritative list of what armed — and hooks_selection_source, which says "plan" if your AGENTVISION_HOOKS reached the runtime or "default (all)" if it did not. 4) Let the program exit, then look for source `av.bootstrap.exit` (Node: `av.node.exit`, which also has `code`). Start present and exit absent means the process did not exit cleanly — that is itself a finding, not a verification failure. 5) av_install_verify() reports `autoloads`; if false, the program only emits when launched through the wrapper. On java/.NET/go/rust/c/c++/shell av_install_verify returns mode "static" and only proves files exist plus the sink is writable — it does NOT prove any lifecycle record will ever be written.
benefit_examples: Nightly ETL run from crontab: actions.jsonl holds forty runs' worth of lines with no boundaries. The start record's run_id and argv let you say the 02:00 run got --full and the 03:10 retry got --incremental, and the three nights with a start record and no exit record are the nights the box OOM-killed it. stdout_tee just concatenates all forty runs; nothing else marks the seam.

Desktop GUI (tkinter/PyQt) the user launches by double-clicking: the report is 'it doesn't open'. The start record answers the only question worth asking first — was a process ever created, with what argv, from what cwd. No start record means the bug is in the launcher or the shortcut, not in the code, and you stop reading the source.

Game loop or emulator with visual_capture on: Python lifecycle records carry frame_seq from .av_frame_seq, so the start record pins 'screenshots from frame 812 onward belong to this run'. Without it a 20,000-frame store from six sessions cannot be split and av_frame_alignment has nothing to anchor to.

Pytest harness invoked hundreds of times in a loop: argv in the start record shows exactly which test selection each run used, and a missing exit record identifies the runs the harness hard-killed on timeout as opposed to the runs that failed an assertion. In the console output those two are indistinguishable.

run_wrapper.one_line: You launch the program yourself with `agentvision run -- <cmd>` and capture its stdout, stderr and exit status from outside the process. The only option for a compiled binary — and it captures nothing if the program is started any other way.
run_wrapper.what_it_does: python_backend/cli.py cmd_run does all of it, at launch time. It scaffolds <project>/agentvision/ if missing; sets AGENTVISION_PROJECT, AGENTVISION_LOG_DIR, AGENTVISION_SINK, AGENTVISION_RUN_ID and prepends agent_bootstrap to PYTHONPATH (and appends NODE_OPTIONS / RUBYOPT if those emitter files exist); writes av.wrapper.start; spawns the child with subprocess.Popen(stdout=PIPE, stderr=PIPE, bufsize=0); runs two reader threads that mirror every line to your terminal and append one JSON record per line, parsed through connectors/log_adapters; runs a background thread that polls every file under the project once a second; forwards SIGINT/SIGTERM/SIGHUP/SIGBREAK to the child; then on proc.wait() writes av.wrapper.exit with the exit code. Nothing is installed into the program. The capture exists only while the wrapper process is alive.
captures: av.wrapper.start (category `process`): run_id, argv (the exact command), project, wrapper_pid.

One JSONL record per stdout line and per stderr line in <project>/agentvision/actions.jsonl. Each line is run through log_adapters.parse_line, so a log4j / serilog / pino / logfmt / glog / spdlog / env_logger line gets a real top-level `category` and `level` plus a parsed `source` (the logger name). An ERROR line printed by a Go or C++ binary becomes category "error" and trips failure detection. data.text always keeps the raw line; data.channel is "stdout" or "stderr".

ts_ms on each line record is the WRAPPER's arrival time — the same clock the bridge stamps screenshots with, which is what makes console lines align to frames. Any timestamp inside the line is preserved separately as data.emit_ts_ms.
av.wrapper.exit: run_id and exit_code. On POSIX a signal death is a NEGATIVE number, because Popen.wait() returns -N: a segfault reads exit_code -11, a SIGKILL -9.
av.wrapper.spawn_fail (category `error`) with the error text and argv when the command does not exist; the wrapper itself returns 127.

FILE-WRITE EVENTS, on by default and not mentioned anywhere in the catalog: a thread polls every file under the project every 1.0 s and emits av.wrapper.file.create / av.wrapper.file.modify / av.wrapper.file.delete (category `file`) with the relative path and mtime_ms. It skips .git, .venv, venv, node_modules, __pycache__, .mypy_cache, .pytest_cache, .ruff_cache, .tox, dist, build, .idea, .vscode, log and any dot-directory. Disable with --no-watch-files or AGENTVISION_WATCH_DISABLE=1; retune with AGENTVISION_WATCH_INTERVAL. For a program whose real product is files, this is often the most useful thing the wrapper gives you.

Environment injection as a side effect: because PYTHONPATH is set to agent_bootstrap, a Python child also gets the full in-process hooks; NODE_OPTIONS / RUBYOPT are appended when agentvision/emitters/av_emit.js or av_emit.rb exist.
Optional: --record-input (or AGENTVISION_RECORD_INPUT=1) also starts the input recorder daemon, detached.
misses: Anything the program does not write to stdout or stderr. A silent binary yields exactly two records plus whatever the file watcher saw.
A segfault leaves only exit_code -11. No stack, no registers, no faulting address. The wrapper is outside the process and cannot look in.

Output that was buffered when the process died. The child's stdout is a PIPE, not a terminal, so C/C++/Go libc switches from line buffering to block buffering (typically 4-8 KB). printf lines that would have appeared on a terminal die unflushed. The lines nearest the crash — the ones you want — are the ones most likely gone. Tell the user to re-run with `stdbuf -o0 -e0`, or setvbuf(_IOLBF), or the language's unbuffered flag, when the tail matters.
Anything written straight to the tty (/dev/tty) and anything written to fd 3 or higher. Only fds 1 and 2 are piped.
Output of grandchildren the child does not forward. Each process you want captured needs its own wrapper.

frame_seq is null on EVERY wrapper record — both _emit_jsonl and _emit_console_line hardcode frame_seq: None. Alignment to screenshots is by timestamp only, unlike the Python in-process emitter which reads .av_frame_seq.

Console line records when the child is python, node or ruby. _child_has_inprocess_emitter keys off the interpreter name in argv[0] and switches the tee to MIRROR-ONLY, so the in-process emitter writes instead and the wrapper adds no per-line records. Selecting run_wrapper for a Python target gets you start/exit/file records only.
Any structured value the program did not print: variables, arguments, return values, exceptions that never reach a stream.

Everything, if the program is launched any other way. Double-clicking the binary, `./app` from a terminal, a systemd or launchd unit, an IDE Run button, a docker entrypoint, a desktop shortcut — zero records, no warning, and the bridge still looks installed. This is by far the most common way this emitter produces nothing.
File changes faster than the 1 s poll (created and deleted between polls) and content changes that leave mtime unchanged.

A single run_id for the whole run when the child is Python: cli.py stamps records with AGENTVISION_RUN_ID while av_runtime builds its own _RUN_ID and never reads that env var, so av.wrapper.* and av.bootstrap.* records from one run carry different run_ids.
run_wrapper.lang_reason: A native binary has no interpreter startup to inject into — no sitecustomize, no --require, no RUBYOPT — so nothing can be loaded in-process without changing the build. The only remaining vantage point is OUTSIDE the process: the pipes on fds 1 and 2, and the wait() status. That is exactly what the wrapper takes, and it is also precisely why it can never see an exception object, a variable or a stack frame — none of those cross the process boundary. Note the menu: bridge_plan._emitter_options offers this id only when the detected language is go, rust, cpp, c, shell or empty/unknown. The mechanism works on any command, and java/.NET are told to fall back to it when nobody wires their config, but on those languages it is not one of the offered ids.

shell pipeline, build script or Makefile step
compiled data pipeline whose output is files
embedded / serial flashing or device tool
any program the user already starts by typing a command
use_when: The project has a build artifact and no entry script: Makefile, CMakeLists.txt, Cargo.toml, go.mod, meson.build, a .vcxproj — and no .py/.js/.rb main. There is nothing to hook in-process.
The target's output is printf / fprintf(stderr / std::cout / fmt.Println / println! / echo, i.e. code_evidence shows `prints_only`, and no log file is written anywhere.
existing_logs_found is empty and code_evidence has no `existing_logging`. There is nothing for an adapter to read, so a log has to be created, and for a binary this is the only creator on the menu.
The user already starts the program from a terminal, so prefixing one command is a change they will actually make. ASK them how they launch it before selecting this.
The program's real product is files it writes (a compiler, a transcoder, an exporter). The file watcher hands you the write timeline for free.
You need the exit status, including the signal number. Nothing running inside a process can report its own SIGKILL or SIGSEGV.
The program shells out — code_evidence `subprocess`, or exec.Command / system( / popen( in the source — and you at least want the parent's console.
The program already prints structured lines (glog, spdlog, zerolog, slog, env_logger, tracing). The wrapper's adapter pass turns those into real levels and logger names instead of raw text.
do_not_use_when: You cannot get the user to change how they launch it: a GUI app started from the Dock or Start menu, a service under systemd/launchd, a container entrypoint, an IDE Run button. Selecting it then records intent and captures nothing. Ask first; if the answer is no, say so in the rationale and pick something else.

The target is python, node or ruby and you want parsed console lines. The wrapper deliberately goes mirror-only for those interpreters — select stdout_tee / logging_bridge / uncaught_exceptions instead.
You need to know why it crashed. This gives you a signal number. Use the program's own crash handler, a core dump, or a debugger.

The program prints tens of thousands of lines a second (a per-frame game log, a packet trace). Every line becomes a JSON record plus an adapter parse; you will fill the sink and the token budget. Reduce the program's verbosity first, or pin a cheap adapter.

The program is a full-screen or interactive terminal app: check for isatty(, termios, tcsetattr, ncurses, curses. stdin is still inherited, but stdout becomes a pipe, so isatty() flips to false — colour disappears, progress bars break, and buffering changes behaviour.

The project tree is large and you leave the watcher on. Note `target/` is NOT in the ignore list, so a `cargo build` inside the wrapper floods the sink with av.wrapper.file.modify records. Pass --no-watch-files.
You have also selected lifecycle expecting more detail. The wrapper already writes both boundary records and its exit record carries the exit code, so the pair is redundant.
run_wrapper.cost: One extra command word at launch. No code change, no build change, no recompile. At runtime: two reader threads, one JSON record plus one adapter parse per console line, and — unless disabled — a full os.walk of the project every 1.0 s. On a big tree the walk is the real cost, and Rust's target/ directory is not in the ignore list, so a rebuild under the wrapper can emit thousands of file records. Use --no-watch-files or AGENTVISION_WATCH_DISABLE=1 there. The human cost is the one that actually matters: someone has to remember the command every single time.
run_wrapper.builds_as: Almost nothing lands in the project. installer.py writes a language note under <project>/agentvision/emitters/ — CPP_README.txt for c/c++, RUST_README.txt for rust, av_emit.go for go, av_emit.sh for shell, and for an unknown language no file at all — plus the standard agentvision/ sinks (actions.jsonl, log.txt, state.json, stats/, crashes/) and manifest.json. None of those capture anything. The capture logic lives entirely in python_backend/cli.py cmd_run and exists only while `agentvision run` is running.
run_wrapper.enforced: RECORDED AS INTENT, twice over. First: go, rust, cpp, c, shell and unknown are all in emitters._ONE_ARTIFACT_LANGS, so selection_report() answers every id with enforced: false and "recorded only — this language builds ONE artifact (config drop-in or stdout/stderr tee)". Nothing in the target program reads your selection; the same README and the same sink files are written whatever you pick. Second, and more important: the capture is not installed at all. It is a behaviour of the `agentvision run` command at launch time. Committing a plan containing run_wrapper changes nothing about the program and starts nothing. What makes it real is the user typing the command, every run. Always hand them the exact string, including their own flags.
run_wrapper.how_to_verify: 1) Actually run it, from the project root: `agentvision run -- ./yourapp --your --flags`. 2) Check the boundary records: av_log_raw(), or grep av.wrapper. in <project>/agentvision/actions.jsonl. You must see source `av.wrapper.start` carrying your argv, and after the program ends `av.wrapper.exit` carrying exit_code. If you find `av.wrapper.spawn_fail` instead, the command path was wrong and the wrapper returned 127. 3) Check console capture: av_log_normalized() or av_log_where() should show records whose source is `av.wrapper.stdout` / `av.wrapper.stderr` (or a parsed logger name) with data.text equal to lines you watched in the terminal. Start and exit present but no line records means either the program printed nothing, or argv[0] was python/node/ruby and the tee went mirror-only. 4) Do NOT trust av_install_verify here: for these languages it returns mode "static", and `verified` there means only "emitter files exist and the sink is writable". It never launches anything and cannot tell you whether capture works. 5) Ask the user to confirm they will start the program through the wrapper every time. If they will not, everything above passes once and the bridge is blind from then on.
benefit_examples: C++ engine or emulator that dies mid-run: the user says 'it just quits'. av.wrapper.exit with exit_code -11 proves SIGSEGV rather than a clean early return or a handled error — a distinction nothing inside the process could report, because no handler got to run. The surviving stderr lines bracket the death, and the file records show which output file it was mid-write on. Then tell the user to re-run under `stdbuf -o0`, because the block-buffered tail is exactly the part that is missing.

Shell release pipeline of a dozen chained commands: the terminal scrollback merges everything and the failing step is ambiguous. Each wrapper line record carries `channel` plus an arrival ts_ms from the wrapper's own clock, so you can reconstruct the true stdout-vs-stderr ordering that the terminal interleaves and reorders, and av.wrapper.exit gives the aggregate status. The file.create/file.modify stream then separates 'step 8 never ran' from 'step 8 ran and wrote a bad artifact'.

Go REST service binary in a plain dev run: it returns 500s and its JSON logger writes to stdout only, so there is no file for any adapter to read. The wrapper's adapter pass turns each ERROR line into category "error" with the logger name in `source`, which is what lets av_errors_by_fingerprint and av_incidents group them at all.

Compiled ETL that writes parquet partitions and prints almost nothing: the failure is 'it stalls'. The av.wrapper.file.create/modify timeline shows which partitions were written, in what order, and which one it stopped on — information that appears in no log, because the program never prints per file. No other emitter in the catalog produces it, and the catalog does not even mention that it exists.

Every check can pass on the day you install it and the bridge can still be blind for the next month, because capture depends on how the program is started. When you select it, state the exact `agentvision run -- ...` command in your message to the user and say plainly that starting the program any other way records nothing.

stdout_tee.one_line: Records every line the program writes to stdout or stderr as its own timestamped JSONL event.
stdout_tee.what_it_does: On Python, av_runtime.install_all_hooks replaces sys.stdout and sys.stderr with _TeeStream (agent_bootstrap/av_runtime.py:178). Each write goes to the real terminal FIRST, then the text is buffered and split on "\n". Every complete line becomes one record: category "stdout" or "stderr", source "av.bootstrap.stdout" or "av.bootstrap.stderr", data {"text": <line>}. flush() emits whatever partial line is left, and the atexit handler flushes both streams. Each record is appended to <project>/agentvision/actions.jsonl and mirrored as one human line into <project>/agentvision/log.txt shaped '<iso> [INFO] [av.bootstrap.stdout] text=<line>' (stderr gets [WARN], from av_runtime._CATEGORY_LEVEL). Every record carries run_id and frame_seq (read from .av_frame_seq, cached 1 second), which is what lets av_actions_around_frame line printed output up with a screenshot. On Ruby the same idea is a $stdout/$stderr wrapper class inside agentvision/emitters/av_emit.rb (source av.ruby.stdout, data.message and data.text). On Node there is NO stdout tee: av_emit.js wraps console.log/info/warn/error/debug only. For every other language nothing is installed in-process; stdout/stderr is captured only when the program is launched through `agentvision run -- <cmd>`, where python_backend/cli.py:_tee reads the child's pipes and emits one adapter-parsed record per line.
captures: Every complete line written through Python's sys.stdout / sys.stderr, including bare print() and any third-party library that prints.

Tracebacks a framework prints instead of raising. Tkinter's report_callback_exception writes a callback traceback to sys.stderr and never calls sys.excepthook, so this is the only emitter that sees it.
stderr separately from stdout: different category, so warning text can be told apart from normal output.
The exact ts / ts_ms and frame_seq of each line, so printed output can be paired with a screenshot.
A trailing partial line with no newline, at flush() time and again at process exit.
misses: Bytes written straight to file descriptor 1 or 2: os.write(1, ...), printf from a C extension, or a child process that inherited the terminal. The tee only sees writes through the Python sys.stdout object.

Everything after something else replaces sys.stdout. contextlib.redirect_stdout and pytest's default capture both do this after the tee installs, so under `pytest` (without -s) the tee records nothing.

Child-process output. Under `agentvision run`, cli.py sets emit_jsonl=False whenever the command starts with "python" (_child_has_inprocess_emitter), so the wrapper only mirrors those bytes to the terminal and writes no record for them.
Blank lines. _TeeStream.write skips empty lines (`if line:`), so a print() of nothing leaves no record.
Log-framework records whose handler writes to a file instead of a stream. logging to app.log is invisible here; that is logging_bridge's job.

Structure. data has one field, "text". Level, logger name and source line are never parsed out. The level word in log.txt comes from the CATEGORY, not the line, so every stderr line is labelled WARN even when it is informational.
Anything the program never prints: a silent early return, a swallowed exception, a hang with no output.
languages: node (partial: console.* only, not the stdout stream)
any other language (only via `agentvision run`, never in-process)
stdout_tee.lang_reason: A real tee is an in-process stream swap, so it needs a runtime that loads AgentVision code before the program's own code: Python (sitecustomize found on PYTHONPATH) and Ruby (RUBYOPT -r). Node cannot be teed by this build because av_emit.js patches the console object, not the stream, so process.stdout.write() passes straight through. A compiled binary (go, rust, c, c++) and a JVM/.NET process have no in-process hook to install at all. The option still appears in the menu for every language because it lives in bridge_plan._emitter_options' `common` list, but for those languages the bytes are captured by the `agentvision run` wrapper pipe, which is the same artifact run_wrapper describes.
use_when: grep of the target finds print( / sys.stdout.write / sys.stderr.write / traceback.print_exc and no logging.getLogger. This is code_evidence signal "prints_only".
The program's only progress information is printed text such as 'processing 1200/5000', and nothing writes it to a file.
The program launches other programs with subprocess.run/Popen and prints their captured output itself. This is code_evidence signal "subprocess".
A GUI toolkit is imported (tkinter, PyQt) whose framework prints callback tracebacks to stderr instead of raising them.
visual_capture is true and printed lines are the only text there is to align with frames.
do_not_use_when: The program's output is a logging framework only: logging.getLogger and logger.info appear, bare print( does not. Choose logging_bridge; the tee would record nothing unless some handler happens to write to a stream.
The target is a compiled binary, a JVM service, or .NET. Selecting this id builds nothing in-process there; choose run_wrapper (or config_dropin) and launch through `agentvision run`.
The target is Node and writes with process.stdout.write, winston or pino. av_emit.js wraps console.* only.
The program prints inside a tight loop, or redraws a progress bar with \r (tqdm). Every flush becomes a record, and each record is two file open/append/close cycles under one global lock.
The target will only ever be exercised under pytest's default capture or inside redirect_stdout. sys.stdout is replaced after the tee installs.
The program already writes a text log that appears in existing_logs_found. Pin it with adapters={"<label>":"auto"} instead of duplicating output into a second sink.
stdout_tee.cost: Per output line: one JSON encode, one open/append/close of agentvision/actions.jsonl, one open/append/close of agentvision/log.txt, all inside a single module-level threading.Lock, plus at most one cached read of .av_frame_seq per second. Threads that print at the same time serialize on that lock. The original write happens before any of this, so terminal output is unchanged and never lost to a sink error (every write path is wrapped in try/except pass). A few lines a second: negligible. Thousands of lines a second, or a \r redraw loop: measurable, and the sink grows fast enough to matter for av_retention.
stdout_tee.builds_as: No file of its own. On Python it is a facet of agent_bootstrap/av_runtime.py (_TeeStream, armed by install_all_hooks when "stdout_tee" is in AGENTVISION_HOOKS); the installer writes <project>/sitecustomize.py with that literal baked in and inserts AgentVision's root into sys.path, so av_runtime is never copied into the project. On Ruby it is the tee class inside agentvision/emitters/av_emit.rb. On Node it is the console wrap inside agentvision/emitters/av_emit.js. For any other language it is python_backend/cli.py's wrapper tee, which runs only under `agentvision run -- <cmd>`. Sinks created either way: agentvision/actions.jsonl and agentvision/log.txt.
stdout_tee.enforced: PYTHON: gated at runtime. install_all_hooks arms the tee only if "stdout_tee" is in AGENTVISION_HOOKS (av_runtime._selected_hooks). Three exact leaks to know about: (1) if AGENTVISION_HOOKS is unset or empty, ALL FIVE hooks arm, and `agentvision run` never sets that variable - only the generated <project>/sitecustomize.py does, and only when CPython actually imports that copy; (2) emitters.hooks_env() returns {} when the plan names no hook ids at all, so a plan that deliberately left stdout_tee out can still get it; (3) if the project already had a sitecustomize.py the installer leaves it untouched and the selection is written nowhere. RUBY and NODE: recorded only. emitters.selection_report now reports enforced=FALSE for them (it used to wrongly say true), because av_emit.rb and av_emit.js contain no AGENTVISION_HOOKS check, so everything in those files is always on. JAVA, .NET, GO, RUST, C, C++, SHELL, UNKNOWN: recorded as intent. One artifact is produced whatever is selected (emitters._ONE_ARTIFACT_LANGS), and the install report says so per id. Leak (2) is now DISCLOSED rather than silent: emitters.hooks_fail_open() returns the list of hooks that will arm anyway, and the install report carries it as emitter_selection_fail_open. Confirm against the av.bootstrap.start record's hooks_armed / hooks_selection_source, which is ground truth.
stdout_tee.how_to_verify: Look for the record, not the install message. (1) av_install_verify(project_root=...): expect events_seen >= 1, and read `autoloads` - if it is false the program emits nothing unless started with `agentvision run -- <cmd>`. (2) In <project>/agentvision/actions.jsonl find the newest record with source "av.bootstrap.start": data.hooks_armed must contain "stdout_tee", and data.hooks_selection_source reads "plan" only when AGENTVISION_HOOKS was actually set, otherwise "default (all)". (3) The real proof is a record with category "stdout" and source "av.bootstrap.stdout" whose data.text is a line you know the program prints - av_search(q="<that line>") or av_log_raw. (4) av_program_log() tails agentvision/log.txt; a live tee shows lines shaped '<iso> [INFO] [av.bootstrap.stdout] text=...'. If step 3 finds nothing while the terminal clearly shows output, the writes are bypassing sys.stdout (fd-level write, or a child process).
benefit_examples: Tkinter desktop GUI: a button handler raises KeyError. Tkinter catches it in report_callback_exception and prints the traceback to sys.stderr, so the window simply stops responding, the process stays alive, and sys.excepthook never fires - uncaught_exceptions sees nothing. stdout_tee records that traceback as category "stderr" with a ts_ms, and av_actions_around_frame shows it beside the frame where the button was clicked.

CLI batch importer with no logging at all: it prints 'row 4193: skipping, bad date' and exits 0 with a wrong row count. The teed stdout records are the only per-row evidence that exists, and because each carries frame_seq they can be paired with the progress frame where the count went wrong.

Wrapper script that calls ffmpeg via subprocess.run(capture_output=True) and prints the child's stderr on failure. 'Invalid data found when processing input' exists in no logger and no exception; the tee is what puts it on the timeline in order with the parent's own lines.

Keypress utility whose entire output is 'pressed: a' per event. Without the tee the JSONL holds only process start and exit, so 'the program never saw the key' and 'the program saw it and did nothing' look identical. The teed lines answer that, with millisecond timestamps to compare against the screen.

stdout_tee.caveat: On Python the menu offers 5 emitters and bridge_plan.blanket_threshold caps a plan at 3, so this slot is spent deliberately. Note the blind spot the wrapper deliberately leaves: under `agentvision run -- python x.py` cli.py declines to emit JSONL for the child's pipes because a python child is assumed to have the in-process emitter. If stdout_tee is then NOT armed, printed output is recorded by nobody - it is only mirrored to the terminal. The raw_output.txt tee in the generated sitecustomize only partly fills that gap: connectors/log_sources.py:613 DOES list <root>/agentvision/raw_output.txt among suggest_log_sources' candidates (adapter='auto'), so it is readable once discovered - but that sitecustomize is not necessarily the copy CPython imports under `agentvision run`, so do not count on the file existing. Verify with av_log_sources rather than assuming either way.

logging_bridge.one_line: Attaches a handler to Python's root logger so every logging call becomes a JSONL event carrying its level, logger name and source line.
logging_bridge.what_it_does: On Python, install_all_hooks adds av_runtime._JSONLHandler to logging.getLogger() (the ROOT logger) with handler level DEBUG, and - only when the root logger's level is still exactly WARNING - raises the root level to INFO. For each record that reaches root it calls self.format(record); no formatter is set, so the stdlib default Formatter is used and data.message is the interpolated message text (with the traceback appended when the call used exc_info or logger.exception). The record's levelno is mapped onto the unified category: >= ERROR becomes "error", >= WARNING becomes "warn", everything else becomes "log". That mapping is the point - a Python ERROR trips AgentVision's failure detection exactly like an ERROR line from any other language. Source is "av.bootstrap.log.<logger name>"; data carries level (the real level word), logger, message, module, func, line. The same record is mirrored into agentvision/log.txt as '<iso> [<LEVEL>] [av.bootstrap.log.<logger>] <message truncated to 2000 chars>'. It attaches exactly once, at interpreter startup, and only if no _JSONLHandler is already on root. Node and Ruby are offered this id but their emitters contain no logging-framework hook at all. Java and .NET are never offered it; their equivalent is the separate config_dropin id.
captures: Every logging call that reaches the root logger - the program's own and third-party libraries' (urllib3, botocore, sqlalchemy) - with data.logger naming whose line it is.
The level twice over: data.level as the real word (DEBUG/INFO/WARNING/ERROR/CRITICAL), and category as error/warn/log, which is what av_incidents and av_diagnose key on.
module, func and line of the call site, enough for av_source_at_error to open the code.
The traceback text of logger.exception() or exc_info=True, because with no formatter set the default Formatter appends the formatted exception to the message.
Messages with the program's own %-args already interpolated - the formatted text, not the template.
misses: DEBUG records, normally. The handler is DEBUG but the ROOT LOGGER's level decides what reaches it, and this hook only raises WARNING to INFO. Unless the program itself sets DEBUG, debug lines are dropped before the handler runs.
Any logger with propagate=False, and any logger whose own level filters the call. Server frameworks commonly configure their loggers that way.

Everything after the program reconfigures logging. logging.config.dictConfig({...,"root":{...}}), logging.config.fileConfig, and logging.basicConfig(force=True) all REMOVE every root handler, this one included. Verified empirically: the handler is gone afterwards, nothing in the codebase re-attaches it (one addHandler call exists, in install_all_hooks), and capture silently stops for the rest of the run. Django settings.LOGGING, uvicorn, gunicorn and celery all configure logging this way at startup.
Bare print() / printf output - that is stdout_tee.
Anything logged before AgentVision loads, i.e. in any process not started through `agentvision run` (or without the emitter env set).

Structured context. Only level, logger, message, module, func and line are copied; extra={...} fields, record.args and stack_info are dropped, and the traceback is buried inside data.message rather than a field of its own.
The logging output of any subprocess the program spawns - each process needs its own hook.
languages: node (offered, but no framework hook is built)
ruby (offered, but no framework hook is built)
logging_bridge.lang_reason: A logging bridge means adding a handler inside the running process, so it needs the language's own logging framework in the same interpreter. Only the Python emitter does that (logging.getLogger().addHandler inside av_runtime.install_all_hooks). Node and Ruby see this id because bridge_plan._emitter_options hands the same `inproc` block to all three, but av_emit.js only patches console.* and av_emit.rb only tees $stdout/$stderr - no winston/pino/Logger hook exists in this build, so selecting it there changes nothing. Java and .NET are excluded from the inproc block entirely: their equivalent is config_dropin, a logback appender or Serilog file sink that the app must be told to load, which is a config file rather than an in-process hook. A compiled binary has no logging framework AgentVision can reach in-process at all.
use_when: grep of the target finds logging.getLogger, logger.info/.warning/.error or logging.basicConfig with a high count. This is code_evidence signal "existing_logging".
Exception handlers already report through a logger (code_evidence signal "logs_in_handler"). The program knows what went wrong; it only needs routing onto the timeline.
The program's handlers write to a file of their own (FileHandler, RotatingFileHandler) or to nowhere, so nothing appears on stdout and a tee would be blind.
The evidence you need belongs to a third-party library - retries, connection resets, deprecations - which are logged and never printed.
The plan needs ERROR/CRITICAL to trip failure detection automatically; the category mapping is what does that.
You have checked and the program does NOT call dictConfig / fileConfig / basicConfig(force=True) after startup.
do_not_use_when: The program never calls logging: no getLogger, no basicConfig anywhere. The handler will sit on root and emit nothing. Choose stdout_tee.

The program or its server reconfigures logging at startup - Django settings.LOGGING, uvicorn/gunicorn log config, celery, or any dictConfig with a "root" section, fileConfig, or basicConfig(force=True). Those detach this handler and nothing puts it back. Pin the framework's own log file with plan.adapters, or use stdout_tee if the framework logs to the console.

The program already writes a log file in a format AgentVision has an adapter for and it shows up in existing_logs_found. Pin it (adapters={"<label>":"auto"}) instead of duplicating every record into a second sink.
The target is Node, Ruby, a JVM or .NET service, or a compiled binary. Nothing is built - see enforced.

The program logs per frame or per row (logger.debug/.info inside a hot loop). Every record is two file appends under one global lock, and the WARNING-to-INFO bump can make the program's own handlers start printing lines it previously suppressed.
The only failures you care about are crashes. A crash reaches no logger; that is uncaught_exceptions.
logging_bridge.cost: Per log record that reaches root: one format() call, one JSON append to agentvision/actions.jsonl, one line appended to agentvision/log.txt, both inside a single module-level threading.Lock (so logging threads serialize), plus a cached .av_frame_seq read at most once a second. Handler failures are swallowed, so the host program is never broken by a sink error. One real side effect on the target, and one that USED to be far worse. Fixed: our root handler made the program's own logging.basicConfig() a no-op (it is documented to do nothing when root already has a handler), so a script whose WARNING/ERROR normally reached the terminal printed NOTHING while every record was still captured - a false read manufactured by the observer. av_runtime._shield_basicconfig now hides our handler for the duration of that call, so the program configures the root it expects. What remains: when the root logger is still at its default WARNING, the hook sets it to INFO, so INFO records now flow to the program's OWN handlers too - a program that called logging.basicConfig() will start printing INFO lines to its terminal that it did not print before. An EXPLICIT level= is respected and capture simply follows it, so a program that chose level=WARNING keeps printing exactly what it did before and INFO is captured by nobody.
logging_bridge.builds_as: No file of its own. It is a facet of agent_bootstrap/av_runtime.py: the _JSONLHandler class plus the single root.addHandler call inside install_all_hooks, armed when "logging_bridge" is in AGENTVISION_HOOKS. The installer writes <project>/sitecustomize.py with the selection baked in and creates agentvision/actions.jsonl, agentvision/log.txt and agentvision/emitters/README.txt. Nothing is added to the program's logging config and no third-party package is needed.
logging_bridge.enforced: PYTHON: gated at runtime. install_all_hooks attaches the handler only if "logging_bridge" is in AGENTVISION_HOOKS (av_runtime._selected_hooks). Same three leaks as the other hooks: an unset or empty AGENTVISION_HOOKS arms ALL FIVE; `agentvision run` never sets that variable (only the generated <project>/sitecustomize.py does, and only when CPython imports that copy - av_install_verify's python probe does put the project root on PYTHONPATH, so the gate is observable there); emitters.hooks_env() returns {} when a plan names no hook ids at all, so an unselected logging_bridge can still arm; and if the project already had its own sitecustomize.py the installer leaves it alone and the selection is recorded nowhere. NODE and RUBY: recorded only. emitters.selection_report reports enforced=true, but av_emit.js and av_emit.rb contain no AGENTVISION_HOOKS check and no logging-framework hook, so the id changes nothing. JAVA / .NET: this id is not even offered - config_dropin is, and it is recorded as intent because one config file is written whatever is selected. Leak (2) is now DISCLOSED rather than silent: emitters.hooks_fail_open() returns the list of hooks that will arm anyway, and the install report carries it as emitter_selection_fail_open. Confirm against the av.bootstrap.start record's hooks_armed / hooks_selection_source, which is ground truth.
logging_bridge.how_to_verify: (1) av_install_verify(project_root=...): events_seen >= 1 proves the emitter loads; autoloads=false means the program emits nothing unless launched with `agentvision run -- <cmd>`. (2) In agentvision/actions.jsonl the newest "av.bootstrap.start" record must list "logging_bridge" in data.hooks_armed, and data.hooks_selection_source says "plan" when AGENTVISION_HOOKS was set, "default (all)" otherwise. (3) The real proof is a record whose source starts with "av.bootstrap.log." - av_search(q="av.bootstrap.log") or av_log_raw - and whose data contains level, logger, module, func and line. (4) Check the mapping: a logger.error call must land with category "error", not "log"; that is what av_incidents and av_diagnose read. (5) av_program_log() tails agentvision/log.txt, where these appear as '<iso> [ERROR] [av.bootstrap.log.myapp.db] ...'. (6) If step 3 finds records early in the run and none after a certain point, look for a dictConfig / fileConfig / basicConfig(force=True) call at that moment - the handler was detached there.
benefit_examples: REST service (Flask/aiohttp): a handler logs logger.warning('upstream 503, retry 2/3') and serves a cached body, so the client sees HTTP 200 and the incident is invisible in the access log. logging_bridge turns it into a category "warn" record with the logger name and exact module/func/line, so av_diagnose flags it and av_source_at_error opens the retry code. A stdout tee catches this only if a StreamHandler happens to be attached; with a FileHandler it catches nothing.

Data pipeline with a RotatingFileHandler: 'chunk 12 checksum mismatch' goes to pipeline.log at WARNING while the dashboard screenshot shows a stalled bar. logging_bridge puts the same record in actions.jsonl WITH frame_seq, which is what lets av_actions_around_frame put the mismatch next to the frozen frame - the separate pipeline.log has no frame correlation at all.

Library-heavy CLI that pauses 30 seconds with no output. urllib3 logs 'Retrying (Retry(total=2, connect=None, ...)) after connection broken' at WARNING and prints nothing anywhere. This is the only emitter that records third-party logger lines, and data.logger names urllib3.connectionpool, so the pause is explained instead of guessed.

PyQt desktop GUI with a worker thread: the worker catches an exception and calls logger.exception('save failed'), and the UI keeps spinning. The record arrives as category "error" with the entire traceback inside data.message (the default Formatter appends it), so the failure is on the timeline even though nothing crashed, nothing printed, and the window looked busy.

logging_bridge.caveat: Two facts a weak model gets wrong here. First, the catalog text for this id says 'python (logging), node, ruby, java (logback), .NET (Serilog)', but java and .NET never receive this id from _emitter_options - do not select it for them; select config_dropin. Second, this bridge is attach-once and any later logging reconfiguration silently removes it, so on a framework-managed service it can appear to work for the first few records and then go quiet with no error anywhere. Verify with a record, not with the commit report. On Python the menu offers 5 emitters and blanket_threshold caps a plan at 3, so pick this only when logging is genuinely how the program speaks.

uncaught_exceptions.one_line: Records the crash itself: the exception that kills the process, the exception that kills a worker thread, and errors during shutdown — each as one structured record with the full traceback.
uncaught_exceptions.what_it_does: PYTHON (agent_bootstrap/av_runtime.py, _install_exception_hooks): replaces sys.excepthook, threading.excepthook and sys.unraisablehook. Each replacement writes ONE JSONL record with category "exception" and then calls the hook it replaced, so the program still prints its traceback to stderr and still exits with the same code (measured: exit=1, traceback still printed). Sources are av.bootstrap.excepthook, av.bootstrap.thread_excepthook, av.bootstrap.unraisablehook. Fields: type, message, traceback (full string), plus thread name for the thread hook and repr(object) for the unraisable hook. Records land in <project>/agentvision/actions.jsonl (AGENTVISION_LOG_DIR, set by the installed sitecustomize and by `agentvision run`), or <project>/log/actions.jsonl if that env var is unset, with a human line mirrored into log.txt tagged [ERROR]. NODE (agentvision/emitters/av_emit.js): registers process.on('uncaughtException') -> av.node.uncaughtException {type,message,stack} and process.on('unhandledRejection') -> av.node.unhandledRejection; if AgentVision is the only uncaughtException listener it re-prints the stack and calls process.exit(1) so default crash behaviour is preserved. RUBY (agentvision/emitters/av_emit.rb): contains NO exception hook of any kind — reading the emitter source, it only tees $stdout/$stderr and emits start/exit.
captures: python: an uncaught exception on the main thread -> av.bootstrap.excepthook with type, message and the full traceback text (measured: ValueError 'top level boom' at app.py:16).

python: an exception that escapes a threading.Thread target -> av.bootstrap.thread_excepthook, including the thread name (measured: 'Thread-1 (w)'). sys.excepthook never sees this one, so nothing else reports it as an exception.
python: errors raised during interpreter shutdown or inside __del__ / weakref callbacks -> av.bootstrap.unraisablehook, with repr of the object involved.
node: an uncaught throw -> av.node.uncaughtException, and a rejected promise nobody caught -> av.node.unhandledRejection with the stack.
The record carries frame_seq (read from log/.av_frame_seq), so a crash can be lined up with the screenshot and log lines around it (av_error_moment, av_source_at_error).
The program's own behaviour is unchanged: previous hooks are chained, stderr still shows the traceback, the exit code is untouched.
misses: EVERY exception the program catches. `try: ... except Exception: pass` produces nothing here. That is swallowed_exceptions' job.
sys.exit() / SystemExit. MEASURED on CPython 3.14: sys.exit(7) does NOT call sys.excepthook — the process just exits 7 and no record is written.

An exception inside an asyncio Task that nobody awaits. MEASURED: it goes to the 'asyncio' logger at ERROR ('Task exception was never retrieved'), not to sys.excepthook. Only logging_bridge sees that.
SIGKILL, SIGSEGV, a C-extension crash, OOM kill, os._exit(). No Python exception object exists, so nothing is written at all — you get silence plus a non-zero exit code.
A hang. A program stuck in a loop raises nothing.

ruby: nothing hook-based. An uncaught Ruby exception is only visible because Ruby prints the backtrace to $stderr and the tee copies those lines — category "stderr", not "exception". You must also select stdout_tee.
Browser JavaScript. av_emit.js loads through NODE_OPTIONS=--require, which no browser reads. A React/Vue/Svelte page needs browser_events.
Anything that fails before the hooks install (a crash inside sitecustomize itself, or a plain `python script.py` where the hooks never load at all).
A crash inside a child process started with subprocess, unless that child is itself launched through `agentvision run`.
uncaught_exceptions.lang_reason: The mechanism is an in-process hook on the interpreter's own exception path — assigning sys.excepthook / threading.excepthook / sys.unraisablehook (python) or process.on('uncaughtException') (node). That path exists only inside a running interpreter, so it is impossible in a compiled binary: go, rust, c and c++ have no interpreter object to patch, and the installer gives them only the stdout/stderr tee, where a segfault leaves no output at all. java and .NET get a logback/Serilog config drop-in, not a hook. The catalog also offers this id when language is ruby, but the installed av_emit.rb contains no exception hook — verified by reading the emitter source — so on ruby this id buys you nothing beyond the stderr tee.
program_kinds: CLI batch job or cron job (nobody is watching stderr)
desktop GUI app with worker threads
data pipeline or scraper with a thread pool
keypress or automation utility with listener threads
anything launched by a launcher, systemd, a double-click, or a scheduler
use_when: The code creates threads: grep for `threading.Thread(`, `Thread(target=`, `ThreadPoolExecutor`, `concurrent.futures`. A crash on a worker never reaches sys.excepthook, and this is the only hook that reports it (catalog signal: `threads`).
The program is long-running: a `while True:` main loop, `app.run(`, `serve_forever(`, `mainloop()`, and the user's complaint is 'it dies' or 'it stops' with no explanation.
The program is started by something that discards stderr: cron, systemd, a .bat/.sh launcher, a desktop shortcut, a supervisor.
code_evidence shows FEW exception_handlers. If the code does not catch errors, its failures arrive as crashes, and crashes are exactly what this captures.
The code defines `__del__`, `weakref.finalize`, or closes sockets/files in destructors — the unraisablehook covers those shutdown-time errors, which normally print an unattributed message and vanish.
The target is node and uses promises / async without a global handler: grep for `async function`, `.then(`, `await` and the ABSENCE of `process.on('unhandledRejection'`.
You already see tracebacks on a terminal, but you need them as records with timestamps and frame_seq so they can be aligned to frames and to the log around them.
do_not_use_when: code_evidence has a high `discards_error` count (`except: pass`, `except ...: return None`, `except ...: continue`). Those failures never become crashes, so this emitter will report nothing. Select swallowed_exceptions instead.
The failing code runs in a BROWSER (React/Vue/Svelte/plain page JS). Select browser_events — this emitter cannot load in a page.
The target is compiled (go, rust, c, c++). The id is not even offered for those languages; run_wrapper is the mechanism there.
The target is a shell script, PHP, java, .NET, swift or kotlin. No hook exists.
The bug you are chasing is a segfault, an OOM kill, a SIGKILL, or a hang. No Python-level exception happens, so this stays silent. Use lifecycle / run_wrapper and read the exit code.

The program is short, single-threaded, and you already have stdout_tee plus a terminal you actually read. The traceback is already captured as stderr text; this adds a structured copy, not new information.
language is ruby and you are NOT also selecting stdout_tee — with no hook in av_emit.rb, the tee is the only path a Ruby crash can reach the sink.
uncaught_exceptions.cost: Negligible. Three attribute assignments at startup; the hook bodies run only when an exception escapes. One appended JSONL line plus one text line per crash. No sampling, no dedupe, no cap — a program that crashes in a restart loop writes one record per crash. It never suppresses the traceback and never changes the exit code, because each hook chains to the one it replaced (measured).
uncaught_exceptions.builds_as: python: NO separate file for this id. It is a branch inside install_all_hooks() in <AV_ROOT>/agent_bootstrap/av_runtime.py, reached either through the generated <project>/sitecustomize.py (written by installer.py) or through PYTHONPATH=<AV_ROOT>/agent_bootstrap (what `agentvision run` sets). node: <project>/agentvision/emitters/av_emit.js, auto-loaded by NODE_OPTIONS=--require, which `agentvision run` injects. ruby: <project>/agentvision/emitters/av_emit.rb, which contains no exception hook.
uncaught_exceptions.enforced: PYTHON: gated at runtime. install_all_hooks() arms it only when 'uncaught_exceptions' is in AGENTVISION_HOOKS (av_runtime._selected_hooks; unset or empty = all five hooks). MEASURED: with AGENTVISION_HOOKS=lifecycle a top-level ValueError produced NO record at all. Two exactness caveats. (1) The gate only bites when AGENTVISION_HOOKS is actually in the environment. The installer bakes your selection into <project>/sitecustomize.py, but `agentvision run` prepends <AV_ROOT>/agent_bootstrap to PYTHONPATH, so CPython imports THAT sitecustomize, which sets no AGENTVISION_HOOKS — so all five hooks arm. Read data.hooks_selection_source in the start record: 'plan' means your selection gated it, 'default (all)' means everything armed regardless. (2) An unrecognised id in AGENTVISION_HOOKS falls back to arming everything, by design. NODE and RUBY: recorded as intent only. build_emitter puts AGENTVISION_HOOKS in run_env for python alone; av_emit.js always installs its exception handlers whatever the plan said, and av_emit.rb installs none. Note that emitters.selection_report() reports enforced=true for node and ruby — that overstates it, because their run_env carries no hooks variable. Leak (2) is now DISCLOSED rather than silent: emitters.hooks_fail_open() returns the list of hooks that will arm anyway, and the install report carries it as emitter_selection_fail_open. Confirm against the av.bootstrap.start record's hooks_armed / hooks_selection_source, which is ground truth.
uncaught_exceptions.how_to_verify: 1) Read the newest av.bootstrap.start record in <project>/agentvision/actions.jsonl (or <project>/log/actions.jsonl if AGENTVISION_LOG_DIR is unset). data.hooks_armed must contain "uncaught_exceptions"; data.hooks_selection_source tells you whether your plan or the default-all path decided. Tool call: av_search(query="av.bootstrap.start"), or av_log_normalized, or grep hooks_armed on that file. If there is no av.bootstrap.start record at all, the hooks never loaded — a plain `python script.py` does not load them (measured: 0 events without PYTHONPATH). 2) Positive proof that it fires: from the project root run `agentvision run -- python -c "raise ValueError('av-probe')"` and look for a record with source av.bootstrap.excepthook and data.message 'av-probe'. 3) node: look for av.node.start in the sink and confirm NODE_OPTIONS contains --require .../agentvision/emitters/av_emit.js. Note av_install_verify() only proves the emitter LOADS (it spawns a do-nothing probe); it raises nothing, so it does not prove the excepthook fires.
benefit_examples: Cron CSV importer (CLI batch): it dies part-way on a UnicodeDecodeError at row 40,000. Cron throws stderr away, so the user only knows 'the import didn't finish' and the destination table is short. The av.bootstrap.excepthook record gives the exception type, message, the exact traceback line, and a timestamp/frame_seq you can pivot from — the difference between 'it failed somewhere' and 'decode of column 7 in file X'.

Desktop GUI with a worker thread (PyQt/tkinter + threading.Thread): the user clicks Export, nothing happens, no dialog, and the app keeps running. The thread's RuntimeError never reaches sys.excepthook, never opens a window, and often scrolls past in a console nobody has. av.bootstrap.thread_excepthook names the exception AND the thread ('Thread-1 (w)' in the measured run), which no other emitter records.

Pygame/SDL game loop: the window closes instantly and the report is 'it just quits'. The excepthook record captures the exception plus frame_seq, so you can look at the last captured frame before the crash instead of guessing which state the loop was in.

Keypress/hotkey automation utility: the keyboard listener thread raises and dies, so hotkeys silently stop responding while the process stays alive and the tray icon looks fine. thread_excepthook is the only record that the listener died and why; stdout is empty, there is no crash, and the exit code is still 0 when the user finally quits.
