a LOW count of `except` lines in code_evidence.exception_handlers — errors are not caught, so they crash
node: an existing process.on('uncaughtException' — the app has its own handler; AgentVision emits and then defers to it
uncaught_exceptions.caveat: Do not read 'no exception records' as 'nothing failed'. With only this hook armed, a caught exception, a sys.exit(), an unawaited asyncio Task failure, a SIGKILL and a segfault all produce exactly nothing. Also: the catalog's `async` code signal argues for this emitter, and on node that is right (unhandledRejection is covered), but on PYTHON it is only half right — measured, an unawaited Task's exception goes to the asyncio logger, so logging_bridge is what catches it.

swallowed_exceptions.one_line: Reports the exceptions the program CATCHES and hides — the `try/except: pass` bugs that never crash, never print, and reach no other hook. CPython 3.12 or newer only.
swallowed_exceptions.what_it_does: agent_bootstrap/av_runtime.py, _install_swallowed_exception_hook(project_root). It claims sys.monitoring tool id 4 under the name 'agentvision', registers a callback for sys.monitoring.events.EXCEPTION_HANDLED, and enables that event. On every handled exception the callback walks the traceback to the INNERMOST frame — the raise site — and also takes the handler's code object filename and function name. It then applies two filters before emitting: SCOPE (the raise file OR the handler file must start with the project root path, and neither may contain 'agent_bootstrap'), and DEDUPE on the key (exception type, raise file, raise line) — emitted at occurrence 1, 10, 100, 1000, then every 5000. Once more than 200 distinct sites are known (AGENTVISION_SWALLOW_CAP), only first occurrences of new sites are emitted. Each record is category "warn", source av.bootstrap.swallowed, with message, type, exception (500 chars), raised_at="file:line", handled_in="file:function", occurrences. At interpreter exit an atexit handler emits one av.bootstrap.swallowed_summary with total_occurrences, distinct_sites, and the top 20 sites with their TRUE counts. The callback body is wrapped in a bare except, so it can never break the host program.
captures: A KeyError raised at app.py:5 inside a loop and caught by `except KeyError: pass` — MEASURED: reported with raised_at app.py:5, handled_in app.py:<module>, at occurrences 1 and 10.

An exception raised INSIDE a library but caught by the project's own handler — MEASURED: JSONDecodeError with raised_at /…/python3.14/json/decoder.py:361 and handled_in app.py:<module>. raised_at points at code you cannot change; handled_in is the line that hid it.

True totals at exit — MEASURED: '34 exception(s) were raised and silently handled across 3 distinct site(s)', with sites[] carrying per-site counts (30, 3, 1). The summary is still emitted when the process dies from an uncaught exception (exit 1).
The type and the message of the hidden exception, not just its location — so 'PermissionError: [Errno 13]' vs 'FileNotFoundError' is visible without re-running anything.
Failures in code paths with no output at all: no stdout, no logger call, no stderr, no non-zero exit. This is the only emitter that sees them.
misses: Non-exception failure. A wrong value returned, a branch never taken, `if err: return None`, an HTTP status checked and ignored, an empty list where data was expected. No exception means no event.

EVERYTHING on Python 3.11 and older. MEASURED on CPython 3.10.19 with the id selected: hooks_requested contained swallowed_exceptions, hooks_armed did NOT, data.catches_swallowed_exceptions was false, and all 34 swallowed exceptions from the same script were invisible. sys.monitoring does not exist there, so the installer returns False and stays silent.

Exceptions raised AND handled entirely inside library code (both paths outside the project root) — filtered out on purpose, so urllib3 retries and optional-import probes do not bury the program's own bugs.
Every non-python language. node, ruby, java, .NET, go, rust, c/c++, shell get nothing; the catalog does not offer the id for them.

Accurate live counts. The live `occurrences` field is the count AT EMISSION — measured 10 in the last live record for a site that really fired 30 times. Only av.bootstrap.swallowed_summary has the truth.
Repeats past the dedupe schedule, and everything except first occurrences once 200 distinct sites are known.
The exit summary if the process is SIGKILLed, segfaults, or calls os._exit — atexit never runs, so you keep only the deduped live records.

Anything at all if another sys.monitoring tool already holds tool id 4 (a debugger, a coverage run): use_tool_id raises, the function returns False, and the only trace is catches_swallowed_exceptions=false.
Any judgement about whether a swallow is a BUG. The hook cannot tell a hidden defect from deliberate control flow, and it reports both.
swallowed_exceptions.lang_reason: The mechanism is sys.monitoring EXCEPTION_HANDLED — a CPython interpreter API that first exists in 3.12. It requires an in-process callback inside the same interpreter, so it is impossible in a compiled binary (no interpreter to instrument), impossible in a logback/Serilog config drop-in (a logging framework never sees an exception nobody logs), and impossible through a stdout tee (a swallowed exception prints nothing). node and ruby have no equivalent event, which is why bridge_plan._emitter_options explicitly strips this id from their menus. On CPython 3.11 and older, hasattr(sys.monitoring.events, 'EXCEPTION_HANDLED') is false and the installer returns False without a word.
program_kinds: data pipeline / ETL that processes many records in a loop
scraper or API client with retries and fallbacks
file, serial, or device tool that wraps I/O in try/except
plugin or optional-dependency loader (`try: import x except ImportError`)
long-running python service whose responses are always 200 but sometimes wrong
config/parser code that falls back to defaults
any python program whose complaint is 'it runs fine but the output is wrong or empty'
use_when: code_evidence.signals contains `discards_error` with a HIGH count — handlers whose body is `pass`, `return None`, `return`, or `continue`. The catalog calls this the strongest possible case for this emitter.
The symptom has no error anywhere: the result is wrong, a field is missing, a file was not written, a row count is short, a feature is silently absent.
The target reads files, sockets, or serial ports inside try/except (catalog signal `file_io`: permission and missing-path errors are often swallowed).
The target parses untrusted input — json.loads, int(), float(), datetime.strptime, yaml.safe_load — inside try/except with a default fallback.
The target loads plugins or optional dependencies with `try: import ... except ImportError: pass` and a capability is mysteriously missing at runtime.
The target retries in a loop and the loop just ends early, or a worker pool completes with fewer results than inputs.

CHECK THE INTERPRETER FIRST. Confirm python >= 3.12 from pyproject.toml requires-python, setup.cfg, .python-version, tox.ini, or a Dockerfile `FROM python:3.12`. If the project pins 3.9/3.10/3.11, do not select this.
do_not_use_when: The target's python is older than 3.12. It arms nothing and you get silence that looks exactly like health — the most expensive way to be wrong here.
code_evidence shows few or no except blocks. Those failures arrive as crashes; select uncaught_exceptions.
The language is not python. There is no mechanism, and the id is not offered.

The project's virtualenv lives INSIDE the project root (.venv/, venv/, env/, or vendored site-packages). The scope filter is a plain startswith on the project path, so every library retry and feature probe under that directory passes it and the report fills with other people's control flow.
A debugger or a coverage run may be attached (debugpy, pytest-cov, pydevd). Another tool can already hold sys.monitoring tool id 4, and then this silently does not arm.
You only need the crash. This emitter is about failures that do NOT crash; the crash path is uncaught_exceptions.

The program's hot path uses an except clause as normal control flow thousands of times per second (e.g. a parse-or-default in an inner loop). The dedupe keeps the LOG small, but the python callback still runs on every handled exception.
The process is normally killed with SIGKILL or a hard stop and you were counting on the exit summary — atexit will not run.
swallowed_exceptions.cost: Near zero when nothing raises. When exceptions do fly, a python-level callback runs on EVERY caught exception in the process, including library control flow, before the scope filter can discard it — the filters bound the LOG, not the callback. Log volume is bounded hard: one record per site at occurrences 1/10/100/1000 then every 5000, at most 200 distinct sites (raise with AGENTVISION_SWALLOW_CAP), plus exactly one summary record at exit. Two small dicts of state (_SWALLOW_SEEN, _SWALLOW_HANDLER) live for the process lifetime. It can be turned off without re-planning: AGENTVISION_CATCH_SWALLOWED=0.
swallowed_exceptions.builds_as: sys.monitoring EXCEPTION_HANDLED hook on tool id 4, inside _install_swallowed_exception_hook() in <AV_ROOT>/agent_bootstrap/av_runtime.py. NO file is written into the target project for this id — it is a branch of install_all_hooks(), reached through the generated <project>/sitecustomize.py or through PYTHONPATH=<AV_ROOT>/agent_bootstrap (what `agentvision run` sets). Its records land in the same sink as every other hook: <project>/agentvision/actions.jsonl, mirrored as text into <project>/agentvision/log.txt.
swallowed_exceptions.enforced: Gated at runtime, and gated TWICE. First, install_all_hooks() arms it only when 'swallowed_exceptions' is in AGENTVISION_HOOKS (unset or empty = all five hooks arm). Second, _install_swallowed_exception_hook can still refuse and return False: python < 3.12, AGENTVISION_CATCH_SWALLOWED=0/false/empty, or sys.monitoring tool id 4 already held by another tool. When it refuses, the id is left out of hooks_armed even though it is in hooks_requested. So selecting it is necessary but never sufficient. MEASURED: AGENTVISION_HOOKS=lifecycle -> catches_swallowed_exceptions=false and no records; AGENTVISION_HOOKS=swallowed_exceptions,uncaught_exceptions on 3.14.6 -> armed, records present; the same env on 3.10.19 -> requested, not armed. Same PYTHONPATH caveat as every python hook: `agentvision run` prepends <AV_ROOT>/agent_bootstrap, whose sitecustomize sets no AGENTVISION_HOOKS, so all five hooks arm and hooks_selection_source reads 'default (all)' instead of 'plan'. Leak (2) is now DISCLOSED rather than silent: emitters.hooks_fail_open() returns the list of hooks that will arm anyway, and the install report carries it as emitter_selection_fail_open. Confirm against the av.bootstrap.start record's hooks_armed / hooks_selection_source, which is ground truth.
swallowed_exceptions.how_to_verify: TWO FIELDS, ONE RECORD. Find the newest av.bootstrap.start in <project>/agentvision/actions.jsonl: data.catches_swallowed_exceptions must be true AND data.hooks_armed must contain "swallowed_exceptions". If it is false or missing, this is NOT WATCHED and silence proves nothing. The plain-text mirror carries the same flag — MEASURED line in <project>/agentvision/log.txt: `[av.bootstrap.start] pid=56833 argv=['app.py'] python=3.14.6 catches_swallowed_exceptions=False`. Tool calls: av_search(query="catches_swallowed_exceptions") for the flag, av_search(query="av.bootstrap.swallowed") for hits. Finally, always read total_occurrences from av.bootstrap.swallowed_summary, never `occurrences` from a live record (measured: 30 real vs 10 reported live).
benefit_examples: ETL / data pipeline (CSV -> database): every row is wrapped in `except Exception: continue`. The run prints '12,000 rows imported' and the table holds 9,800. Nothing crashes, nothing logs, exit code 0. This emitter names the site — ValueError raised at transform.py:88, handled in loader.py:run — and the exit summary's total_occurrences IS the count of missing rows. No other emitter produces a single byte about this.

Embedded / serial tool: the read loop does `try: port.read() except Exception: pass`, so a USB device that renumerates is indistinguishable from an idle device. The record shows SerialException raised inside pyserial's serialposix.py and handled_in reader.py:poll — the handler line is the one to fix. stdout is empty, there is no crash, and the logger was never called, so stdout_tee, logging_bridge and uncaught_exceptions all see nothing.

This emitter shows the real cause (e.g. FileNotFoundError on a config the action opens) at occurrence 1, and the true press count in the exit summary. Note the scope: it reports the FAILURE of the handler, not the keypress itself — no emitter records physical input today.

REST service (FastAPI/Flask): a dependency wraps its cache/DB lookup in try/except and returns a default, so every response is 200 with stale or empty data. The access log looks perfect and the error log is empty. This emitter shows ConnectionError raised inside redis/connection.py, handled_in deps.py:get_cache, thousands of occurrences — a 200-only request log can never show that.

swallowed_exceptions.caveat: MEASURED SURPRISE — a crashed worker thread is reported as 'swallowed'. In the 3.14 run, RuntimeError('worker died') escaped a threading.Thread target and appeared as av.bootstrap.swallowed with handled_in threading.py:run, because CPython's threading machinery catches it internally in order to call threading.excepthook. Its summary count was 3 for ONE raise, since it was re-handled at several frames. Two consequences: (1) a swallowed record whose handled_in sits inside the standard library or a framework may be a genuine crash rather than a hidden bug — cross-check av.bootstrap.thread_excepthook; (2) read per-site occurrences as 'times handled', not 'times the bug happened'. Also note handled_in is file:FUNCTION with no line number, while raised_at is file:LINE.

config_dropin.one_line: Writes one logging-framework config file (logback XML for Java, Serilog JSON for .NET) that routes the app's OWN logger output into AgentVision's sink. The file does nothing until you point the app at it and restart.
config_dropin.what_it_does: The installer writes exactly ONE file into the target project. Java gets <project>/agentvision/emitters/logback-agentvision.xml: a complete logback <configuration> holding one FileAppender named AGENTVISION, whose <file> is ${AGENTVISION_SINK:-agentvision/actions.jsonl}, whose encoder pattern emits one JSON object per line, and whose <root level="INFO"> references only that appender. .NET/C# gets <project>/agentvision/emitters/serilog-agentvision.json: a "Serilog" appsettings section using Serilog.Sinks.File, MinimumLevel Information, path "agentvision/actions.jsonl", plus a "_csharp_snippet" string showing ReadFrom.Configuration. That is the whole build. The file is INERT on its own. To make it work you must (a) have the dependency present (logback-classic on the classpath; the Serilog and Serilog.Sinks.File NuGet packages), (b) tell the app to use it (java -Dlogback.configurationFile=<path>, or <include> it from the existing logback.xml; for .NET merge the Serilog section into appsettings.json and call ReadFrom.Configuration), and (c) restart the process, because both frameworks read config only at logger initialization. Lines land in agentvision/actions.jsonl, which the installer pins to the `jsonl` adapter under the label "events".
captures: Java: every event the ROOT logger accepts at INFO or above, as one JSON line per event, with ts (millisecond ISO string), ts_ms (%d{UNIX_MILLIS}, a real epoch-millis number), level, source = the logger name, data.message, data.thread, and data.logger.
.NET: every Serilog event at Information or above, as one JSON line per event, with ts (ISO string), level, source = SourceContext, and data.message.

Whatever the app already reports through slf4j/logback or Serilog: handled-and-logged exceptions, warnings, request lines, business events. This is a ROUTING emitter, not a discovery one - it moves existing log output onto the AgentVision timeline.
misses: Anything not written through the logging framework. System.out.println, System.err, Console.WriteLine, printf, native/JNI writes, and a third-party library bound to a different backend (log4j2 directly, java.util.logging with no slf4j bridge, Microsoft.Extensions.Logging with no Serilog provider) all bypass the appender completely.
Everything logged before the logger is configured: static initializers, JVM/CLR startup, a Spring Boot banner and bootstrap phase, and any crash during class loading.
DEBUG and TRACE. The Java config sets <root level="INFO"> and the .NET config sets MinimumLevel Information. Anything below those levels is dropped, not written.

Stack traces. Neither template contains a throwable converter - the Java pattern has no %ex/%throwable/%xThrowable, and the .NET outputTemplate has no {Exception}. So an exception's stack does not appear inside data.message.
Any failure that produces no log line at all: a SIGKILL, an OOM kill, a JNI segfault, a bare System.exit, or a thread that dies without logging. The appender writes only what a logger call gives it.
log4j2. The emitters.py module docstring says "logback / log4j2", but build_emitter() writes only logback-agentvision.xml. There is no log4j2 artifact anywhere in this build.

.NET only: the sink path is the literal relative string "agentvision/actions.jsonl" and the config never reads AGENTVISION_SINK. It resolves against the process working directory, which for `dotnet run` or a published binary is usually bin/<Config>/<tfm>/. So the file is often created at bin/Debug/net8.0/agentvision/actions.jsonl while AgentVision reads <project_root>/agentvision/actions.jsonl and sees nothing.

.NET only: the outputTemplate hardcodes "ts_ms":0 and "category":"log". Every .NET record therefore carries ts_ms 0, which breaks tools that filter on ts_ms (av_actions_around_frame windows on ts_ms).

Correct escaping. The Java pattern escapes only the double-quote character in the message, via %replace(%msg){'"','\\"'} - a message containing a backslash or a newline produces a malformed JSON line. The .NET template drops {Message:lj} between two literal quotes with no escaping filter at all.

A trustworthy ISO timestamp. Both %d{yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ss.SSS'Z'} and {Timestamp:yyyy-MM-ddTHH:mm:ss.fffZ} print the local clock and then append a literal Z claiming UTC. On a non-UTC machine the ts string is wrong by the UTC offset. Java's ts_ms is still correct; .NET has no usable ts_ms.
Java only: the category field is filled from %.-1level, a one-character slice of the level, so category is a single letter rather than an AgentVision category name like "error" or "log".
config_dropin.lang_reason: The mechanism is a config FILE read by a logging framework at startup, so it only exists where such a framework exists: logback on the JVM, Serilog on .NET. There is no in-process hook and nothing is injected, so it cannot apply to a compiled binary or to Python/Ruby/Node. The catalog gates the option on the detected language string being EXACTLY "java", "dotnet", or "csharp" (bridge_plan.py line 118), with no alias expansion. So a project detected as "kotlin" or "scala" (from .kt files, per bridge_plan._EXT_LANG) is never offered this option, even though emitters._LANG_ALIASES would map kotlin/scala/jvm to java and fsharp/vb to dotnet if it were selected. For those projects use the stdout tee via `agentvision run` instead.
use_when: A logback.xml, logback-spring.xml, or logback-test.xml already exists under src/main/resources - the app is already a logback app and you can <include> the AgentVision appender into it.
pom.xml or build.gradle lists logback-classic, or any spring-boot-starter (which pulls logback in transitively).
Source files import org.slf4j.Logger / org.slf4j.LoggerFactory and call LoggerFactory.getLogger(...).
A .csproj lists Serilog, Serilog.Sinks.File, or Serilog.AspNetCore; or Program.cs contains new LoggerConfiguration() or UseSerilog(); or appsettings.json already has a "Serilog" section.

catalog.code_evidence.signals.existing_logging has a HIGH count and logs_in_handler is non-zero. That combination means the program already reports its own errors properly - you only need to route them somewhere readable, which is exactly what this emitter does.
You control the launch command (you can add a -D flag) or you can edit appsettings.json, AND you can restart the process. Without both, the file you write changes nothing.
do_not_use_when: The project uses log4j2 (a log4j2.xml file, or a log4j-core dependency). No log4j2 config is produced, so selecting this builds a logback file the app will ignore.
The project logs only through java.util.logging, or only through Microsoft.Extensions.Logging with no Serilog provider registered. The appender never receives those events.
The process cannot be restarted, or you cannot change its launch flags / appsettings. Config is read once at logger init.

The failure you are chasing is plain console output. If code_evidence.signals.prints_only is high and existing_logging is low, the program prints instead of logging - the framework never sees it. Use the stdout tee (`agentvision run -- java -jar app.jar`) instead.
The bug happens during startup, before the logger is configured, or is a hard crash with no log line (OOM, segfault, kill).
You need DEBUG or TRACE detail. Both templates floor at INFO/Information and there is no knob in the generated file to change that without editing it by hand.
The detected language is kotlin, scala, fsharp, or vb. The option is not offered for those strings at all.
You are on .NET and you need frame-to-log time alignment. Every .NET record has ts_ms 0, so it cannot be windowed against a screenshot timestamp.
config_dropin.cost: Cheap to build, not free to wire. Building it writes one file (a few KB) into <project>/agentvision/emitters/ and costs nothing at runtime. Wiring it costs: one dependency (logback-classic on the classpath, or two NuGet packages), one launch flag or one appsettings merge, and one process restart. RUNTIME cost after wiring is one buffered file append per log event - the same order as the app's existing file appender. IMPORTANT SIDE EFFECT ON THE JVM: passing -Dlogback.configurationFile=<this file> REPLACES the app's whole logback configuration, and the generated <root> references ONLY the AGENTVISION appender - so for that run the app's own console and file appenders and all its per-logger levels are gone. To keep them, <include> this file's appender from the existing logback.xml and add an <appender-ref> instead.
config_dropin.builds_as: One file, overwritten on every install. Java -> <project>/agentvision/emitters/logback-agentvision.xml. dotnet/csharp -> <project>/agentvision/emitters/serilog-agentvision.json. Written by installer.install_into_project via emitters.build_emitter, which sets kind="config" and verify="emitter_present" on the EmitterSpec. Nothing else is generated: no code, no wrapper, no second file per selected id.
config_dropin.enforced: RECORDED AS INTENT. java, dotnet, and csharp are all listed in emitters._ONE_ARTIFACT_LANGS, so emitters.selection_report() returns {enforced: false, how: "recorded only - <lang> builds ONE artifact (config drop-in or stdout/stderr tee); this id is a facet of it, not a separate build"} for every id in the plan. config_dropin is also absent from emitters.HOOK_SELECTABLE, so hooks_env() never produces an AGENTVISION_HOOKS value for it - and AGENTVISION_HOOKS is read only by the Python runtime (agent_bootstrap/av_runtime.py), which is not involved here. Concretely: selecting config_dropin, or selecting it together with stdout_tee and lifecycle, produces byte-for-byte the same one file. The plan records your judgement; it does not change the build.
config_dropin.how_to_verify: Four steps, in order, because the first three can all pass while the emitter is still dead. (1) FILE EXISTS: `ls <project>/agentvision/emitters/` shows logback-agentvision.xml or serilog-agentvision.json. (2) MANIFEST AGREES: <project>/agentvision/manifest.json has emitter.kind == "config", the file listed in emitter.files, emitter_selection_enforced == false, and an emitter_selection entry for config_dropin with enforced false. (3) DO NOT TRUST av_install_verify HERE: for java/dotnet, _probe_spec returns None, so /install/verify takes the static path and returns mode:"static", events_seen:0, and verified:true whenever agentvision/emitters/ is non-empty and actions.jsonl is writable. That green light says nothing about whether the config is wired. (4) THE ONLY REAL PROOF: start the app with the config applied, make it log one line, then call av_log_raw() or av_log_normalized() and look for a record whose source is your logger name or SourceContext - on Java also confirm data.thread and data.logger are present and ts_ms is a large non-zero number. Equivalently, check that <project>/agentvision/actions.jsonl grew. IF NOTHING ARRIVED ON .NET, look for bin/<Config>/<tfm>/agentvision/actions.jsonl first: the hardcoded relative path is the single most common reason the file is written somewhere AgentVision is not reading.
benefit_examples: Spring Boot REST service returning intermittent 500s. Its @ExceptionHandler already logs an ERROR for every one, but into a rotating file nobody opens. The drop-in puts each event on the AgentVision timeline with data.thread, which reveals that all the failures come from a single http-nio worker thread - a per-thread pattern that a stdout tee flattens away and that no screenshot can show.

.NET background worker (IHostedService) that quietly stops draining its queue. Serilog Information lines arrive with SourceContext, so you can read the last class that logged before the silence and measure exactly how long the gap is. Nothing else tells you WHICH component went quiet, because the process is still alive and exits cleanly.

A JVM batch job run nightly from cron, where the scheduler discards stdout entirely. The appender writes to the file sink regardless of where stdout goes, so the run appears on the timeline at all - the difference between "we can see the job ran and what it did" and "we have no record it ever started".

A Java desktop app (Swing/JavaFX) that freezes. Screenshots show a stuck window, and the Java pattern emits ts_ms from %d{UNIX_MILLIS}, so av_actions_around_frame can window the logger events against the exact frame where the UI stopped repainting. This is the one config drop-in variant that supplies usable epoch millis; the .NET one writes ts_ms 0 and cannot do this.
code_signals: grep -rl 'org.slf4j' src/ - slf4j imports mean the app logs through the facade logback backs
grep -rn 'LoggerFactory.getLogger' src/ - real logger call sites, and how many
ls src/main/resources/logback*.xml - an existing logback config to <include> from instead of replacing
grep -n 'logback-classic\|spring-boot-starter' pom.xml build.gradle build.gradle.kts - the dependency must already be there
grep -rn 'log4j2\|log4j-core' pom.xml build.gradle src/ - a HIT here argues AGAINST this emitter; no log4j2 artifact is produced
grep -rn 'Serilog' *.csproj Program.cs appsettings.json - Serilog already present on .NET
grep -rn 'UseSerilog\|new LoggerConfiguration' Program.cs Startup.cs - the wiring point you will edit
grep -rn 'System.out.println\|Console.WriteLine' src/ - many hits argue for the stdout tee instead, because the framework never sees these
grep -rn 'ILogger<\|Microsoft.Extensions.Logging' - .NET logging with no Serilog provider will not reach the sink
config_dropin.caveat: Two catalog inconsistencies to know about. First: java/dotnet/csharp are NOT offered run_wrapper by _emitter_options (that id is gated on go/rust/cpp/c/shell/unknown), yet stdout_tee's own note tells you to use run_wrapper for a compiled program. The stdout tee is still available for the JVM and .NET - it is just reached through the CLI (`agentvision run -- java -jar app.jar`) rather than through a menu id. Second: the java and dotnet menus contain exactly THREE options (stdout_tee, lifecycle, config_dropin), and blanket_threshold(3) is 3, so validate_plan rejects a plan selecting 3 or more. On these two languages you may select AT MOST 2 emitter ids.

browser_events.one_line: A JavaScript file that runs INSIDE the browser tab, catches the client-side failures no server log ever sees (uncaught errors, unhandled promise rejections, console.error/warn, failed fetch/XHR, CSP blocks, dead /
browser_events.what_it_does: agent_bootstrap/av_browser.js is an immediately-invoked function that installs six hooks in the page and batches what they produce. It reads its endpoint from the script tag's data-av-endpoint attribute, else window.AGENTVISION_ENDPOINT, else the default http://127.0.0.1:7771/browser/ingest, and its session id from data-av-session (default "default"). It keeps native references to fetch, XMLHttpRequest, console.error and console.warn BEFORE wrapping anything, so its own transport can never re-enter its own instrumentation. Every 1500 ms (FLUSH_MS) it POSTs the queued records as newline-delimited JSON, and on visibilitychange-to-hidden or pagehide it flushes via navigator.sendBeacon, the only transport that survives unload. Server side, POST /browser/ingest requires every record to carry av:"browser" (records without it are rejected and counted as missing_av_browser_marker, so the route cannot be used to inject arbitrary lines), stamps received_ms so a page with a wrong clock cannot claim the future, and appends to <ACTIVE PROFILE's project_root>/agentvision/log.txt. connectors/adapters/browser.py registers BrowserAvJsonAdapter (name browser_av_json) BEFORE the generic jsonl adapter so it claims those lines and keeps the browser fields instead of flattening them.
captures: Uncaught errors. A window "error" listener registered with capture=true emits level ERROR, category "error", source = the throwing module's basename parsed out of the stack, message "<Name>: <message>", and data.uncaught=true, data.error_class, data.stack (clipped to 2000 chars), data.file, data.line, data.col.

Failed resource loads. When that same "error" event fires on an ELEMENT rather than window (ev.target has a tagName), it emits ERROR, category "network", source = the lowercased tag name, message "failed to load : ", and data.resource_url, data.tag. This is the 404'd ,

Unhandled promise rejections. A window "unhandledrejection" listener emits ERROR, category "error", message "Uncaught (in promise) <Name>: <message>" (or the reason clipped to 400 chars when it is not an Error), and data.unhandled_rejection=true, data.error_class, data.stack. On a modern app this is the most common real failure and it never reaches the server log.

console.error and console.warn. Wrapped to emit ERROR/category "error" and WARN/category "warn". Arguments are stringified (an Error becomes "Name: message", an object is JSON.stringify'd, anything else String()'d), data.console records which function fired, and data.stack is taken from the first Error argument. The original console function is still called with the same arguments and its return value is returned unchanged.

Failed fetch, both kinds. A resolved response with res.ok false emits ERROR when status >= 500 else WARN, category "network", source = the request URL's host, message "<METHOD> <url> <status> (<statusText>)", and data.http_method, data.url, data.status, data.reason, data.duration_ms. A REJECTED fetch emits ERROR, source "fetch", message "<METHOD> <url> failed: <message>", and data.network_error=true, data.error_class, data.duration_ms - this is the CORS, DNS, offline, or abort class, which the server has no record of at all. The response is passed through and the rejection is re-thrown unchanged.

Failed XMLHttpRequest. open/send are wrapped and a "loadend" listener emits, for status 0, ERROR "<METHOD> <url> failed (no response)" with data.network_error=true; and for status >= 400, ERROR when >= 500 else WARN with data.status, data.reason, data.duration_ms. Requests to the ingest endpoint itself are skipped so the transport cannot loop.

Content-Security-Policy violations. A document "securitypolicyviolation" listener emits WARN, category "security", source "csp", message 'Refused to load \'<blockedURI>\' because it violates the Content Security Policy directive: "<violatedDirective>"', and data.blocked_url, data.directive, data.effective_directive, data.document_url.
Page context on EVERY record: url (location.href), user_agent (navigator.userAgent), viewport ("<innerWidth>x<innerHeight>"), ts (ISO) and ts_ms (epoch millis).

An arming announcement. On load it pushes INFO, category "process", source "agentvision.browser", message "browser emitter armed (session=<id>)" with data.endpoint, data.session, and data.captures listing all eight hook names, then flushes immediately. This is the record you check for instead of inferring success from silence.

Repeat counts. Identical level|category|source|first-200-chars-of-message bumps a counter instead of queueing another copy, and the count is attached as data.repeat on the flushed record - so a page stuck in an error loop produces one record with repeat: 400, not 400 records.
misses: console.log, console.info, console.debug. Deliberately not wrapped (volume, no signal). If the app reports state through console.log, this emitter sees none of it.
Every successful request. A 200 response carrying a wrong or empty body is completely invisible - res.ok true emits nothing.
All user input. Keystrokes, form values, clicks and mouse movement are deliberately never captured, because the records ship to a local file. There is no keypress or input capture in this emitter.
Anything before the script executes. An error thrown by a module that loads earlier, or a failure during HTML parse, happens before the listeners exist.
Any other JavaScript realm. The listeners are attached to THIS document's window and document, so a Web Worker, a Service Worker, a cross-origin iframe, and any other tab are all invisible.

Errors the app catches itself. A React error boundary, or a try/catch around a fetch, absorbs the failure - unless that handler also calls console.error or console.warn, this emitter never learns about it.
Framework internals. No component tree, no props or state, no route changes, no render counts, no timing or performance data.

Whatever the caps discard. The queue holds 200 events and drops the OLDEST when full (a WARN "<N> event(s) dropped: queue full (cap 200)" is appended so the loss is visible). Messages are clipped at 2000 chars with a trailing "…[clipped]". Only 50 distinct signatures are tracked per flush window, so a 51st repeating error is queued in full every time instead of collapsing. Server side the route rejects past 500 records per POST, past 8000 bytes per record, and returns 413 BODY_TOO_LARGE past 2,000,000 bytes.

Its own failures - by design, and this is the dangerous one. Safety rule 2 forbids logging a transport error, because an emitted transport error would loop until the tab died. So if the bridge is down, the port is wrong, or CORS blocks the POST, the page keeps working normally, nothing appears in the console, and AgentVision simply receives nothing. Silence here does NOT mean the app is healthy.
The last events before a hard tab crash. A renderer OOM runs no unload handler, so the final 1500 ms of queued records are lost.

Readable stack frames in a production bundle. The stack regex extracts whatever the bundle reports and there is no source-map lookup, so on a minified build source_file and source_line point into main.<hash>.js, not into your .tsx. This is a dev-build emitter.
Everything server-side. It is the client half only - a 500 thrown inside your API handler is reported here only as the status the browser saw.
browser_events.lang_reason: The catalog offers this option only when the detected language string is one of node/javascript/typescript/ts/js (bridge_plan.py line 135). The mechanism itself is a <script> tag or an import inside a browser page: it needs window, document, and navigator.sendBeacon, so it cannot run in a compiled binary, in a Python/Ruby/JVM/.NET process, or even in Node - Node has no window. The mirror image is why this option had to exist at all: the Node emitter's mechanism is NODE_OPTIONS=--require, a SERVER-side preload that a browser can never honour, so before browser_events a React/Vue/Svelte app was offered an emitter that physically could not load in the place its failures happen.
use_when: An index.html exists, or a browser entry file does: src/main.tsx, src/main.js, src/index.jsx, app/layout.tsx, App.vue, App.svelte.
package.json lists react and react-dom, or vue, or svelte, or @angular/core - or has a dev-server script (vite, next dev, react-scripts start, webpack serve).

Source files call fetch( or axios or new XMLHttpRequest AND touch the DOM in the same tree (document., window., useEffect). That combination means the requests you care about are issued from the browser, where only this emitter can see them fail.
catalog.code_evidence.signals.async is non-zero in front-end files. Unhandled promise rejections are the failure this emitter is best at, and nothing else in AgentVision sees them.
The complaint is "the page is blank" or "the button does nothing" while the server log shows nothing but 200s. That gap IS the client half, and this is the only emitter that covers it.

You can add one script tag or one import to a DEV build, AND the page can reach the bridge over HTTP - same machine on 127.0.0.1:7771, or data-av-endpoint pointed at a host the page can actually reach.
do_not_use_when: The project is a Node server, a CLI tool, or a library with no browser page. No index.html and no DOM code means nothing will ever load the script. Pick uncaught_exceptions or logging_bridge for the Node process instead.
It is a production build served to real users. The emitter POSTs to 127.0.0.1 and ships page URLs and stack traces into a local file. Dev builds only.

The page cannot reach the bridge - a remote staging host, or a Content-Security-Policy whose connect-src does not allow the endpoint. It then fails SILENTLY and you will read the quiet log as a healthy app. Note the trap: a CSP strict enough to block the POST also blocks the emitter from reporting that it was blocked.
You cannot add a script tag or an import to the entry module (no access to the template, no build step you control).
The failure is server-side and the server already logs it. A 500 from your own API is in the server log with its stack; this only adds that the client saw a 500.
You need input capture - keypresses, typed values, clicks. This emitter records none of them, deliberately.

The AgentVision active profile points at a DIFFERENT program. The route appends to that profile's project_root/agentvision/log.txt, so your browser events land in another program's log; if that profile has no project_root the POST returns 409 NO_PROJECT_ROOT and everything is dropped.
You are only chasing a build or type error. Those are already covered by the frontend_build_error adapter reading the dev server's own output - no page emitter needed.
browser_events.cost: One <script> tag or one import in the entry module of a dev build. No dependency, no build-system change, no bundler plugin. In the page it wraps console.error, console.warn, window.fetch, and XMLHttpRequest.prototype.open/send, and adds three window listeners plus one document listener. All of it is bounded: a 200-event queue, 2000-char messages, 50 tracked signatures, and at most one POST per 1500 ms (mode cors, keepalive true). Every handler is wrapped in try/catch so it can never throw into the host page, and every wrapped API returns and rejects exactly as before. THE REAL COST IS A MANUAL STEP: the installer does not ship this file. You must copy it into the app yourself and serve it (for example to public/agentvision/av_browser.js) before anything is captured.
browser_events.builds_as: NOTHING IS GENERATED. This is the field to read twice. The catalog text says it builds "agentvision/emitters/av_browser.js", but no code writes that file: installer.py contains no browser branch, and emitters.build_emitter for node/javascript/typescript returns files={"emitters/av_emit.js": <the Node preload shim>} and nothing else. A repo-wide grep for av_browser finds it only in agent_bootstrap/av_browser.js (the source), bridge_plan.py (this catalog text), bridge_server.py (comments on the ingest route), and a test that checks the catalog WORDING. So: the emitter source already exists at <AgentVision>/agent_bootstrap/av_browser.js and you must copy it into the target project and serve it from the dev server yourself. What the install DOES produce for this language is <project>/agentvision/emitters/av_emit.js, which is the SERVER-side Node shim loaded via NODE_OPTIONS - it cannot run in a browser and it is not this emitter.
browser_events.enforced: RECORDED AS INTENT, and not even wired. browser_events is absent from emitters.HOOK_SELECTABLE and absent from agent_bootstrap/av_runtime._HOOK_IDS (which holds only stdout_tee, logging_bridge, uncaught_exceptions, swallowed_exceptions, lifecycle), so hooks_env() never produces an AGENTVISION_HOOKS value for it. "node" is not in emitters._ONE_ARTIFACT_LANGS either, so emitters.selection_report() falls through to its last branch and returns {enforced: false, how: "recorded only - this id maps to no runtime hook in this build, so selecting it changes nothing"}. AGENTVISION_HOOKS is read only by the Python runtime in any case; the generated Node emitter never looks at it. Selecting this id records your decision in the plan. Arming it is a manual step you must perform: copy the file, serve it, add the tag.
browser_events.how_to_verify: Six checks, because every earlier one can pass while the emitter is still dead. (1) SERVED: open http://<dev server>/agentvision/av_browser.js in a browser and confirm it returns the JavaScript, not a 404. (2) LOADED: in the page's console, window.__AGENTVISION_BROWSER__ is true. (3) ARMED RECORD ARRIVED - this is the load-bearing check: av_log_raw(), or grep 'browser emitter armed' <project_root>/agentvision/log.txt, shows a line containing "av":"browser", "category":"process", "source":"agentvision.browser", a message starting 'browser emitter armed (session=', and data.captures listing eight hook names. That record is pushed and flushed on load, so its ABSENCE means either the script never ran or the POST never arrived. (4) ROUTE ACCEPTED IT: the POST response body is {"ok":true,"accepted":<N>,"rejected":0,"written":true,"sink":"<...>/agentvision/log.txt","adapter":"browser_av_json"}. accepted 0 with reject_reasons.missing_av_browser_marker means something other than this emitter posted. (5) PARSED CORRECTLY: av_log_normalized() shows records whose data.adapter is "browser_av_json" - the adapter stamps its own name in. If the browser fields are flattened away, the generic jsonl adapter took the source instead. (6) END TO END: from the page console run Promise.reject(new Error("av test")) and confirm that within about two seconds a record appears with data.unhandled_rejection true. DO NOT use av_install_verify as evidence here: for language "node" _probe_spec probes agentvision/emitters/av_emit.js with NODE_OPTIONS, so verified:true there proves the SERVER shim works and says nothing at all about the browser emitter.
benefit_examples: React/Vite SPA whose cart page renders blank while the server log shows only 200s. This emitter records "TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'items')" with data.uncaught true, source "Cart.tsx" (the basename parsed from the stack), plus data.line, the url the user was on, and the viewport - so you learn it is the cart route on a narrow window, and that the API was never the problem. Nothing server-side could have told you any of that.

Analytics dashboard behind a newly tightened Content-Security-Policy: the chart area is simply empty, with no error in any log. The CSP hook emits WARN/security/csp 'Refused to load \'https://cdn.example/chart.js\' because it violates the Content Security Policy directive: "script-src"' with data.blocked_url and data.directive. This failure produces no request, no server entry, and no thrown exception - this emitter is the only thing in AgentVision that can see it.

A browser canvas/WebGL game that stutters and then freezes. The engine's console.warn floods, and repeat-collapsing turns 400 identical "WebGL: too many active contexts" warnings into one record with data.repeat 400 instead of drowning the log - while ts_ms on every record lets the freeze be lined up against the exact captured frame where rendering stopped.

A Next.js app whose Save button silently does nothing on a flaky connection. The fetch rejection branch records ERROR "POST /api/save failed: Failed to fetch" with data.network_error true, data.error_class "TypeError", and data.duration_ms. The server has NO record of this request whatsoever - CORS, DNS failure, offline, and aborts never reach it - so without this emitter the evidence does not exist anywhere.

A Vue admin panel where one table row 404s its avatar. The element branch of the error listener records ERROR/network, source "img", message "failed to load img: /uploads/u/9931.png" with data.resource_url. A broken image is not a JS error, produces no console output, and is served by a different host than your API - so it appears in no log at all otherwise.
code_signals: ls index.html public/index.html src/main.tsx src/main.js app/layout.tsx - a browser entry point is the precondition
grep -n 'react-dom\|"vue"\|svelte\|@angular/core' package.json - it is a front end, not a server
grep -n 'vite\|next dev\|react-scripts start\|webpack serve' package.json - there is a dev build you can add a tag to
grep -rn 'fetch(\|axios\|new XMLHttpRequest' src/ - client-side requests, the failures only this emitter sees
grep -rn 'await \|\.then(\|async ' src/ - promise-heavy code, where unhandledrejection is the dominant failure
grep -rn 'console.error\|console.warn' src/ - the app already reports its own client errors; this routes them
grep -rn 'Content-Security-Policy\|connect-src' - a CSP exists, which is BOTH a reason to use the CSP hook and a risk that it silently blocks the POST
grep -rn 'ErrorBoundary\|componentDidCatch' src/ - errors are being caught; confirm the handler also calls console.error or this emitter will not see them
grep -rn 'new Worker(\|serviceWorker' src/ - hits here mark a BLIND SPOT, not a reason: worker realms are not covered
browser_events.caveat: Menu size depends on the exact language string, and it changes what you are allowed to pick. If the detected language is "node" the menu is five options (stdout_tee, lifecycle, uncaught_exceptions, logging_bridge, browser_events) and blanket_threshold(5)-1 caps a plan at 3 ids. If it is literally "typescript", "javascript", "ts", or "js", bridge_plan's per_lang table has no entry for those keys, so uncaught_exceptions and logging_bridge are NOT offered at all - the menu is just three (stdout_tee, lifecycle, browser_events) and the cap is 2. In practice a TypeScript project is usually detected as "node" anyway, because bridge_plan._EXT_LANG maps .ts and .js to "node". For a full-stack app the useful pairing is browser_events for the client half plus one in-process Node emitter for the server half - but only the Node one is actually gated and built; the browser one you must install by hand.

recipes.shape: A long-running Java or .NET backend service that already logs through logback / log4j2 / Serilog / Microsoft.Extensions.Logging. Headless, started by systemd / Docker / IIS, expected to stay up for days. Its real failure mode is a request path that starts erroring at 03:00 while the process stays alive — so the question is never "did it crash" but "what did its own logger say, and can AgentVision read it".
how_to_recognise: MANIFEST (this is what actually sets the catalog's menu): pom.xml, build.gradle, build.gradle.kts or settings.gradle at the project root -> connectors/log_sources.py::detect_language returns "java". Any of *.csproj, *.sln, *.fsproj, *.vbproj, global.json, Directory.Build.props, nuget.config -> "dotnet". A bare tree of .java/.kt/.scala/.groovy or .cs/.fs/.vb with no build file lands the same way via the extension census.

LOGGING FRAMEWORK, by file: src/main/resources/logback.xml or logback-spring.xml or log4j2.xml; a dependency line containing logback-classic, log4j-core, slf4j-api or net.logstash.logback. .NET: PackageReference to Serilog, Serilog.Sinks.File, Serilog.Sinks.Console or NLog; a "Serilog" section in appsettings.json; `Log.Logger = new LoggerConfiguration()` in Program.cs; `ILogger<Foo>` constructor injection.

LONG-RUNNING, by file: @SpringBootApplication / spring-boot-starter-web; WebApplication.CreateBuilder + app.Run() in Program.cs; a Dockerfile whose ENTRYPOINT/CMD is `java -jar` or `dotnet Foo.dll`; a .service unit; a Kestrel/Tomcat port in config. No mainloop(), no BrowserWindow, no __main__ script.

CODE EVIDENCE to confirm rather than assume: catalog.code_evidence.signals should show `existing_logging` with a HIGH count and example files, `web_service` non-zero, `threads` non-zero (Task.Run / ExecutorService), and `gui_toolkit` ABSENT. `existing_logging` high + `gui_toolkit` zero is the fingerprint that separates this shape from every other one here.

EXISTING LOG FILES: check catalog.existing_logs_found before deciding anything. suggest_log_sources only looks in <root>, <root>/log, <root>/logs and <root>/agentvision for *.log / *.jsonl (and *.txt only if log-named or inside a log dir). If logs/app.log shows up there, its pin LABEL is the file STEM — "app" — not "app.log" and not the path.
recipes.why_each: config_dropin, and nothing else. The strongest signal in code_evidence is `existing_logging` (the regex matches logback/log4j/Serilog/slf4j) — this program is not short of log statements, it is short of a sink AgentVision reads. config_dropin is the only offered id whose artifact touches the framework those statements go through: installer.py writes agentvision/emitters/logback-agentvision.xml (a FileAppender to ${AGENTVISION_SINK:-agentvision/actions.jsonl}) or serilog-agentvision.json (a Serilog File sink). It is also the only java/.NET id that can reach a service you cannot relaunch by hand. THREE THINGS YOU MUST DO OR IT SILENTLY WRITES NOWHERE. (1) The path in both artifacts is RELATIVE, resolved against the JVM/.NET working directory, while installer.py registers the profile source as the ABSOLUTE <project>/agentvision/actions.jsonl — under systemd or Docker those are different files, so set AGENTVISION_SINK to the absolute path in the unit/compose env. (2) The app must be pointed at the config (`-Dlogback.configurationFile=...`, or ReadFrom.Configuration for the Serilog section) — and the logback artifact declares `<root level="INFO">` with ONLY the AGENTVISION appender, so using it AS the main config replaces the service's own console/file appenders; `<include>` the appender from the existing logback.xml if you want both. (3) It needs a restart; that is stated in the catalog's `cost` and it is a real operational cost for this shape. ENFORCEMENT, honestly: java and dotnet are in emitters._ONE_ARTIFACT_LANGS, so this selection is RECORDED INTENT, not a gated build — installer.py writes that one config file whatever the plan says, and emitters.selection_report() will say so per id ("recorded only — java builds ONE artifact"). av_install_verify on java/.NET returns mode="static": it checks only that the emitter file exists and the sink is writable. It cannot tell you the service ever wrote a line.
recipes.deliberately_not: stdout_tee — on java/.NET it installs nothing (one-artifact language), and this shape is started by systemd/Docker, so `agentvision run` (the only thing that actually tees) is never in the picture. Selecting it would record coverage that no process will ever produce. If you DO control the launch, run the wrapper for real (`agentvision run -- java -jar app.jar`, which does adapter-parse every stdout line) instead of naming the id. NOTE the catalog gap while you are here: java/dotnet are NOT offered run_wrapper at all (bridge_plan only adds it for go/rust/cpp/c/shell/unknown), so the tee has no id to select on this shape. lifecycle — the logback/Serilog artifact emits no start/exit record of any kind; it only writes what the app logs. The exit code you actually want comes from cli.py's av.wrapper.exit record, i.e. from the wrapper, not from this id — and the catalog says selecting both is not additive. logging_bridge and swallowed_exceptions are not on the java/.NET menu at all (bridge_plan only adds the in-process trio for python/node/ruby); do not invent them.
recipes.adapters: Do not pin anything at commit time — with config_dropin the installer pins for you: profile_overrides.log_sources becomes events -> jsonl (agentvision/actions.jsonl) and textlog -> auto (agentvision/log.txt). VERIFY AFTER THE FIRST REAL RUN, because both hand-rolled templates have specific defects you must see with your own eyes. .NET: _DOTNET_SERILOG's outputTemplate hardcodes "ts_ms":0. The jsonl adapter treats the line as an AgentVision-native record and only backfills ts_ms when it is None — 0 is not None — so every Serilog record keeps ts_ms=0 forever, which sorts it to 1970 in av_timeline and to the front of av_search as the "oldest" hit. Frame/log alignment for that source is dead until you edit the template to emit real epoch millis. Java: the logback pattern renders ts_ms from %d{UNIX_MILLIS} (fine if your logback version knows that keyword — if it does not, the literal text lands inside the JSON and the line stops being JSON), sets "category" to %.-1level ("I"/"E"/"W", not an AgentVision category — the top-level "level" is correct, which is what _detect_failure_records reads), and escapes only the double-quote in %msg. It also contains no exception converter and no %nopex, so how a logged throwable is rendered is not pinned by this config: after your first real error, look in the sink for bare `at com.foo.Bar(...)` lines sitting outside the JSON. If they are there, either write an adapter with av_add_adapter and pin it, or say in plan.rationale that you accept the weaker parse — a source the catalog reported as uncovered is a hard commit-time rejection otherwise. THE OTHER BRANCH, often the better one: if catalog.existing_logs_found already lists the service's own file log (logs/app.log -> label "app"), prefer emitters:[] with adapters={"app":"auto"} and a rationale containing the word "already" (validate_plan requires "already" or "no log" for an empty emitter list). That is a zero-touch bridge: no config change, no restart, no template defects. Test the pin first with av_test_adapter on a real line from that file and check is_fallback=false, that `level` matches the line, and that `source` is your logger name and not the adapter's own name.
recipes.visual_capture: FALSE. code_evidence has a `web_service` signal and no `gui_toolkit` signal; there is no window, and frames of an empty desktop would burn disk and tokens for nothing. Set it explicitly — it is enforced downstream: with visual_capture=false, av_capture_start returns HTTP 200 with started:false and error VISUAL_CAPTURE_DISABLED_BY_PLAN. That is the plan working, not a fault. Do not pass force=true to "fix" it. Because visual capture is off, every frame tool (av_get_frame, av_latest_frame, av_visual_changes, av_error_moment, av_read_screen, av_ocr_frame) is dead weight for this program — av_error_moment and av_source_at_error both list frames_on_disk in their `needs`, so they will answer emptily forever here. Say that in plan.tools.not_relevant rather than leaving it to be discovered.
recipes.what_would_still_be_invisible: Everything the framework never sees. (1) Anything logged BEFORE config load — Spring's early bootstrap, static initialisers, a failure to read appsettings.json — and anything written outside the logger (System.out.println, Console.WriteLine, a JVM `OutOfMemoryError` dump, the `Picked up JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` line). The catalog states this in config_dropin's `misses` and it is the most common way a startup crash goes unrecorded. (2) A caught-and-logged-at-DEBUG exception when the appender's root level is INFO: the artifact hardcodes INFO, so DEBUG detail is discarded at the source, not filtered at read time. (3) Exceptions the service catches and does not log at all — java/.NET have no swallowed_exceptions equivalent in this build; only python does. (4) A SIGKILL / OOM-kill / container eviction: the logger writes nothing and no lifecycle record exists on this shape, so the log simply stops mid-stream. av_log_where is the tool that tells you the difference between "the service went quiet" and "we are reading a file it stopped holding open" — it asks the OS for the process's real descriptors instead of trusting config. (5) Per-request latency and non-2xx rates unless the app logs them as lines; /metrics endpoints are not logs and nothing here scrapes them. (6) Whether your selection was enforced: it was not — re-read install.emitter_selection in the commit response rather than assuming the plan describes what is running.

recipes.shape: A desktop GUI app with NO logging at all — tkinter, PyQt/PySide, or SwiftUI. Prints occasionally, if that. It fails by looking wrong (a stuck spinner, a stale label, a button that does nothing) or by a callback dying inside the event loop while the window stays up. The screen holds state that no file contains.
how_to_recognise: PYTHON GUI, by import: `import tkinter` / `from tkinter import ttk`; PyQt5 / PyQt6 / PySide2 / PySide6; kivy; wx. Plus a loop entry point: `root.mainloop()`, `sys.exit(app.exec())`, `app.exec_()`. Files/manifests: main.py or app.py or gui.py at root, *.ui designer files, requirements.txt naming PyQt/PySide, a PyInstaller *.spec. detect_language -> "python" via pyproject.toml/requirements.txt or the .py census.

SWIFTUI, by file: *.xcodeproj / *.xcworkspace, Package.swift, ContentView.swift, `@main struct App: App`, Info.plist. WARNING, verified: log_sources has no Swift marker and .swift is not in its extension census, so detect_language returns "" for a pure Swift tree. The catalog then offers stdout_tee + lifecycle + run_wrapper (the "" branch). If somebody has set profile.language="swift", bridge_plan._emitter_options offers only stdout_tee + lifecycle and run_wrapper disappears even though the tee is the ONLY mechanism that exists for a compiled app bundle — and emitters.build_emitter has no "swift" branch, so it falls through to the tee spec with files={} (nothing is written into the project at all). Read what the catalog actually returned; do not assume the menu.

THE ABSENCE IS THE SIGNAL: code_evidence.signals should show `gui_toolkit` non-zero (the regex covers tkinter|PyQt|PySide|kivy|wxPython|SwiftUI|Cocoa|GLFW|SDL|imgui), `existing_logging` ZERO or near it, `prints_only` maybe non-zero, `web_service` absent. gui_toolkit present + existing_logging empty is exactly this shape; gui_toolkit present + existing_logging high is a different (easier) program.

existing_logs_found will be EMPTY. That is the thing to notice: with no logging and no emitter, a commit is refused with BRIDGE_WOULD_READ_NOTHING, and the escape hatch (visual_capture=true plus "visual only" in the rationale) is a worse bridge than installing one cheap emitter.
recipes.why_each: stdout_tee is the load-bearing one, for a reason specific to GUI toolkits rather than for the `prints_only` signal. Verified in this machine's CPython: tkinter.Tk.report_callback_exception prints "Exception in Tkinter callback" and traceback.print_exception to sys.stderr — it does NOT call sys.excepthook, and the mainloop keeps running. So a widget callback that dies produces stderr text and nothing else: uncaught_exceptions never fires, the process never exits, and only the stderr tee (av_runtime._TeeStream wrapping sys.stderr) records it. The same holds for any toolkit that catches inside its dispatch loop and prints. uncaught_exceptions covers the two failures the tee cannot attribute: the crash BEFORE the loop starts (sys.excepthook, with a full traceback as one structured record instead of scattered stderr lines) and a dead worker thread (threading.excepthook) — GUI code pushes work off the UI thread constantly, and a thread that dies leaves a frozen-looking window with no output at all. ENFORCEMENT on python is real but conditional. installer.py bakes AGENTVISION_HOOKS="stdout_tee,uncaught_exceptions" into the generated <project>/sitecustomize.py and av_runtime._selected_hooks() reads it, so only those two arm — BUT only when CPython imports THAT copy, which needs the project root on PYTHONPATH. `agentvision run` prepends <AV_ROOT>/agent_bootstrap to PYTHONPATH, whose sitecustomize sets no AGENTVISION_HOOKS, so all five hooks arm instead. Read data.hooks_selection_source in the av.bootstrap.start record: "plan" means your two gated it, "default (all)" means everything armed. Two more leaks worth knowing: an unset/empty AGENTVISION_HOOKS arms all five by design, and if the project already had its own sitecustomize.py the installer leaves it untouched and your selection is written nowhere.
recipes.deliberately_not: logging_bridge — existing_logging is ZERO. There is no logging call to bridge; the handler would attach to a root logger nobody uses, and a plan that selected it would be claiming to route output that does not exist. If the app is Qt and uses qDebug/QLoggingCategory instead of Python logging, note that av_runtime attaches a logging.Handler only — it never installs a Qt message handler, so logging_bridge cannot see Qt's own diagnostics at all. swallowed_exceptions — select it ONLY if code_evidence.discards_error comes back with a real count, not because it sounds useful: it needs CPython 3.12+, _install_swallowed_exception_hook can still refuse and return False (AGENTVISION_CATCH_SWALLOWED=0, or sys.monitoring tool id 4 already held by a debugger/coverage), and on a small GUI the volume is mostly toolkit internals filtered out by its project-scope check. lifecycle — av_runtime emits av.bootstrap.start unconditionally, whatever the plan says, so selecting lifecycle only adds the atexit half; and for a GUI closed by the window manager or killed from the dock, atexit may never run. Note also that the python exit record carries only {"pid"} — no exit code, despite the catalog's `captures` text saying "exit code". THE THIRD SLOT: python offers 5 emitters, so validate_plan rejects at 4 and you may select up to 3. Leave the third empty here. Two hooks cover the two ways this shape dies.
recipes.adapters: Nothing to pin. There is no pre-existing log, so the only sources are the two sinks the installer creates and wires itself (events -> jsonl for agentvision/actions.jsonl, textlog -> auto for agentvision/log.txt). AFTER the first run, call av_log_sources and then av_test_adapter on a real line from log.txt — av_runtime writes that mirror as `2026-07-30T…Z [LEVEL] [av.bootstrap.stderr] message`, a format nothing in the registry was written for, so check whether auto-detection lands on a named adapter or a fallback. Do not pin blind: the catalog's warning is measured — a C engine's `[DEBUG] Sprite.c:32 - msg` was claimed by coreboot_cbmem at 1.00 confidence and buried the file:line inside the message. If the tee's stderr lines route only to a fallback, either write an adapter with av_add_adapter and pin it under "text", or accept the weaker parse in the rationale; the structured events sink is jsonl and is fine regardless.
recipes.visual_capture: TRUE — this is the shape where frames genuinely earn their place, and it is the only recipe here where I would say that unreservedly. The bug IS the pixels: a label showing yesterday's value, a modal opened behind the main window, a spinner that never stops. code_evidence's gui_toolkit signal is exactly what bridge_plan says argues for visual_capture: true. ASK THE USER for the interval and pass it as capture.interval_seconds (the commit honours it at capture start; an explicit interval on av_capture_start wins over it): ~1s for a form-and-dialog app, 0.1-0.2s if the complaint is about an animation, a drag, or a flicker. Then reach past pixels where you can: av_ui_tree / av_ui_diff read the OS accessibility API (AXUIElement / UI Automation / AT-SPI) and give exact element text, roles and coordinates with no OCR guessing, at a fraction of a screenshot's tokens — their `needs` are accessibility_api + gui_program, not capture_running, so they work even between frames. On macOS that needs the Accessibility TCC grant.
recipes.what_would_still_be_invisible: 1) STATE THAT IS NEVER RENDERED AND NEVER PRINTED. A wrong value living in a widget attribute or a view model shows up nowhere: not in the tee, not in the accessibility tree if it is not displayed, not in a frame. 2) A HANG. If the UI thread blocks, there is no exception, no print, and no change on screen — the only evidence is av_visual_changes reporting long "identical" runs and frames that stop differing. That is a real signal, but you have to go looking for it; nothing raises it. 3) THE USER'S OWN INPUT — the biggest hole on this shape. daemon/input_daemon.py records keyboard and mouse into the active profile's action_log_file and can tell injected events from physical ones (macOS: kCGEventSourceUnixProcessID==0; Windows: LLKHF_INJECTED/LLMHF_INJECTED; Linux: per-device uinput-vs-real-HID), but PHYSICAL events are DROPPED unless the profile's capture_user_input flag is on — and that flag is not an emitter, is not in the catalog, and cannot be named in a plan. To get it you must (a) have the daemon running (started from the GUI Permissions tab or `python -m python_backend.cli daemon start`; on macOS an Accessibility grant; `agentvision run --record-input` also starts it) and (b) flip the flag via av_create_profile — and POST /profiles does `profiles[name] = ProgramProfile.from_dict(data)`, a FULL REPLACE, so sending {"capture_user_input": true} alone WIPES project_root, log_sources and capture_app. Read the whole profile with av_active_profile first and send it back intact. Check av_daemon_status to see whether events are actually flowing. So on a GUI app, "what did the user click just before it broke" is reachable but nothing in the planning surface tells you it exists. 4) A GUI TOOLKIT THAT REPLACES YOUR HOOKS. av_runtime installs at interpreter startup and chains the previous excepthook; an app that later does `sys.excepthook = my_handler` (routine in Qt apps) REPLACES AgentVision's and it goes blind, and logging.basicConfig(force=True) or logging.config.dictConfig clears root handlers, dropping the _JSONLHandler. Nothing re-attaches. If the start record shows the hooks armed but no exception ever lands, suspect this before suspecting the bridge. 5) On SwiftUI: essentially everything in-process. There is no in-process emitter for Swift; you get `agentvision run -- ./Foo.app/Contents/MacOS/Foo` stdout/stderr, frames, and the accessibility tree. os_log/Unified Logging output does NOT go to stdout and is not captured by anything here.

recipes.shape: A data pipeline or batch job that runs to completion and exits — an ETL script, a nightly report, a dbt/Airflow task, a training or migration run. Started by cron, a scheduler, or CI, not by a human. It usually fails by SUCCEEDING WRONGLY: exit 0, 4,000 rows quietly skipped by a per-row `except: continue`. Nothing crashes, so nothing crash-shaped is ever recorded.
how_to_recognise: ENTRY POINT, by file: a script named etl.py / ingest.py / build_*.py / nightly_*.py with `if __name__ == "__main__": main()` and argparse or click; NOT a server and NOT a window. Manifests: a Dockerfile whose CMD is `python etl.py`, a k8s CronJob or crontab line, a Makefile target, dags/ with `DAG(` or `@task` (Airflow), luigi/prefect imports, dbt_project.yml + models/.
DATA-SHAPED IMPORTS: pandas, pyarrow, polars, sqlalchemy, psycopg2, boto3, requests in a loop over records, csv/json readers, `to_parquet`/`COPY`/`bulk_insert`.

CODE EVIDENCE is what makes this shape decidable: `discards_error` with a REAL count (its regex catches `except ...:` followed by pass / return None / return / continue) is the diagnostic signal — that is the per-row swallow. Alongside it expect `file_io` and often `subprocess` non-zero, `exception_handlers` high, and `web_service` and `gui_toolkit` both ABSENT. Weigh the counts: discards_error seen once is nothing; seen thirty times in three files is the whole case.
WHETHER IT ALREADY LOGS decides the second emitter: `existing_logging` high (logging./getLogger) -> logging_bridge; `prints_only` instead -> stdout_tee, but read the tqdm caveat below first.
recipes.why_each: swallowed_exceptions is the point of this recipe and the reason this shape is not shape 2. It answers directly to the `discards_error` signal — bridge_plan itself says that signal is "the strongest possible case for it". av_runtime installs a sys.monitoring EXCEPTION_HANDLED callback (tool id 4), scopes it to files under project_root so urllib3's retry logic is not reported as your bug, dedupes by (type, raise_file, raise_line), and — the part that matters for a batch job — emits av.bootstrap.swallowed_summary at exit with the TRUE totals. The live records are decimated on purpose (emitted at occurrence 1, 10, 100, 1000, then every 5000), so their `occurrences` is the count at emission time; only the summary tells you a defect fired 40,000 times. Nothing else in AgentVision can see these: they never reach stderr, never reach the excepthook, and the job exits 0. IT IS GATED TWICE, so verify rather than assume: install_all_hooks arms it only if it is in AGENTVISION_HOOKS, and _install_swallowed_exception_hook can still return False on CPython < 3.12, with AGENTVISION_CATCH_SWALLOWED=0/false/empty, or if another tool already holds monitoring tool id 4 (a debugger, or coverage under CI — a real risk for a job that runs in a test harness). When it refuses, the id appears in hooks_requested but NOT in hooks_armed, and data.catches_swallowed_exceptions is false in the start record. Silence is not evidence of no swallows unless that field says true. logging_bridge is the cheap second half when existing_logging is high: the job's own INFO lines are where the row counts and file names live, and _JSONLHandler maps levelno >= ERROR to category "error" so a logged failure trips _detect_failure_records the same way any other language's does. It also raises the root level from the default WARNING to INFO, so those count lines actually flow — without it a plain run drops them. Swap logging_bridge for stdout_tee if the job only prints. ROUTE MATTERS MORE THAN USUAL HERE, and it is an EITHER/OR: `PYTHONPATH=<project> python etl.py` imports the project's generated sitecustomize, so your two-hook selection is what runs (hooks_selection_source="plan"); `agentvision run -- python etl.py` prepends <AV_ROOT>/agent_bootstrap to PYTHONPATH, so agent_bootstrap's sitecustomize wins, no AGENTVISION_HOOKS is set, and ALL FIVE hooks arm — but you gain the wrapper's av.wrapper.exit record with the real exit_code. sitecustomize is imported once from the first match on sys.path, and cli.py appends any pre-existing PYTHONPATH AFTER the bootstrap dir, so you cannot have both. Decide which you want and put it in the scheduler.
recipes.deliberately_not: uncaught_exceptions — this is the one shape where the crash is the EASY case. If the job dies, the scheduler already has the traceback on stderr and a non-zero exit status, and the wrapper records exit_code; spending a selection slot on the loud failure while the quiet one goes unwatched is precisely backwards for a job that fails by exiting 0. Reconsider only if code_evidence shows a real `threads` or `subprocess` count — a ThreadPoolExecutor worker that dies never reaches the main excepthook, and threading.excepthook is inside uncaught_exceptions. stdout_tee when the job shows progress — av_runtime._TeeStream splits its buffer on "\n" ONLY, so a tqdm/rich progress bar written with carriage returns accumulates in the buffer and lands as one enormous record at flush. That is worse than not capturing it. lifecycle — av.bootstrap.start is emitted regardless of selection, and the python exit record contains only {"pid"}: no exit code, no duration, contradicting the catalog's `captures` text. For a batch job the exit code is the whole question, and it comes from `agentvision run`'s av.wrapper.exit, not from this id. Do not select lifecycle expecting to learn how the run ended.
recipes.adapters: Two branches, and check existing_logs_found before choosing. IF the job already writes logs/etl.log or log/run.jsonl, the zero-touch answer may be better than any emitter: emitters:[] plus adapters={"etl":"auto"} — the label is the file STEM (log_sources.suggest_log_sources labels each find with `c.stem`), a wrong key is rejected outright, and a rationale for an empty emitter list MUST contain "already" or "no log" or validate_plan refuses it. But an emitters:[] plan writes NOTHING into the project — installer.py only runs when plan.emitters is non-empty — so if that pin does not resolve to a real existing file you get BRIDGE_WOULD_READ_NOTHING and the commit is refused (correctly). Also note the discovery blind spot: suggest_log_sources looks only in <root>, <root>/log, <root>/logs and <root>/agentvision. A job that writes to /var/log/etl/ or to an S3 prefix is NOT discovered, cannot be pinned through the plan at all, and needs the path added to profile.log_sources instead. IF you install the emitters above, the installer pins events -> jsonl and textlog -> auto itself; leave plan.adapters empty and verify afterwards with av_test_adapter on a real line. Either way, if the catalog flagged a discovered source as uncovered (only a fallback claimed its lines), you must write an adapter with av_add_adapter and pin it, or state in the rationale that you accept the weaker parse — otherwise `source` degrades to the fallback's own name on every line and av_errors_by_fingerprint groups every error together while every call keeps returning 200.
recipes.visual_capture: FALSE, and unlike shape 1 this one is worth stating loudly because a batch job often DOES have a terminal. There is no window whose pixels carry state; screenshots of scrolling text cost frames and OCR to recover bytes you already have as structured events. Expect and accept VISUAL_CAPTURE_DISABLED_BY_PLAN from av_capture_start (HTTP 200, started:false) — that is the decision being honoured. Consequence to record in plan.tools.not_relevant: every tool whose `needs` include frames_on_disk or capture_running is inert here — av_error_moment, av_source_at_error, av_visual_changes, av_replay, av_read_screen, av_ocr_frame, av_diff, av_wait_for (it needs capture_running as well as a log source), av_token_report, av_retention.
recipes.what_would_still_be_invisible: 1) CORRECTNESS. A wrong number is not an event. A pandas dtype coercion that turns "00123" into 123, a join that silently drops unmatched rows, a truncated float — none of these raise, none print, and no hook exists for "the output is wrong". swallowed_exceptions catches the failures the code noticed and hid; it cannot catch the failures the code never noticed. If the pipeline writes row counts or checksums into agentvision/state.json, av_state_diff can at least diff two moments — otherwise this whole class is outside the bridge. 2) THE SUMMARY ITSELF, IF THE JOB IS KILLED. av.bootstrap.swallowed_summary and the exit record are emitted from an atexit handler: os._exit, SIGKILL, an OOM-kill, or a container timeout skips it entirely, so you keep the decimated live records (occurrences=1, 10, 100…) and lose the true totals. A partial run's swallow counts are floors, not counts. 3) SWALLOWS BELOW 3.12 OR WITH TOOL ID 4 TAKEN. Check data.catches_swallowed_exceptions; measured behaviour is: AGENTVISION_HOOKS=swallowed_exceptions on 3.14 -> armed, records present; identical env on 3.10 -> requested, not armed, zero records, no error. 4) A JOB THE SCHEDULER LAUNCHES WITHOUT EITHER ROUTE. `python etl.py` from cron with no PYTHONPATH and no wrapper emits NOTHING — the project-root sitecustomize is not found because CPython's site imports sitecustomize before the script's own directory joins sys.path (measured on Homebrew python and a clean venv alike; it is in the installed README). The bridge will look built and the sink will stay empty. 5) CHILD PROCESSES. `subprocess.run(["psql", ...])` output goes to the child's own stdout; the parent's tee never sees it. Wrap the child in `agentvision run` too, or capture= its output and log it yourself. 6) WALL-CLOCK REGRESSION. Nothing here times stages; a job that took 40 minutes instead of 4 is only visible as a gap between timestamps that you have to notice yourself (av_timeline will show it if you look).

recipes.shape: A compiled Go or Rust binary that ALREADY emits structured JSON logs — slog/zerolog/zap/logrus with a JSON formatter, or tracing-subscriber with .json(). Nothing needs to be created; the job is to get lines that already exist onto AgentVision's timeline WITHOUT touching the build, and to notice the two record classes that this path parses wrongly.
how_to_recognise: MANIFEST: go.mod at root -> detect_language "go"; Cargo.toml -> "rust". A tree of bare .go / .rs files gets there by census too.

STRUCTURED LOGGING, by import/dependency: Go — `log/slog` with slog.NewJSONHandler, github.com/rs/zerolog, go.uber.org/zap (zap.NewProduction), sirupsen/logrus with `SetFormatter(&logrus.JSONFormatter{})`. Rust — tracing + tracing-subscriber with features=["json"] in Cargo.toml and `.json()` on the fmt subscriber, or env_logger (text, NOT json — different answer).

WHERE IT WRITES, which decides the whole recipe: grep for os.Stdout / io.MultiWriter / os.OpenFile / File::create / a --log-file or --log-dir flag. Then look at catalog.existing_logs_found: a *.jsonl or *.log in <root>, log/, logs/ or agentvision/ means there IS a file to read (label = its STEM) and each such entry carries `covered` / `detected_adapter` from AgentVision sampling its real lines. Empty existing_logs_found + JSON-to-stdout means the wrapper is the only route.

CODE EVIDENCE: `existing_logging` high (fmt.Print / println! / slog match its regex), `gui_toolkit` and `web_service` per the actual program, primary_language go or rust. The catalog menu for both is exactly three ids — stdout_tee, lifecycle, run_wrapper — so validate_plan rejects at 3 and you may select at most 2. One is the right answer here.
recipes.why_each: run_wrapper, alone — and only for the stdout case.
