There is no in-process hook to install in a native binary, so `agentvision run -- ./target/release/app` is the entire mechanism: cli.py's tee reads each line, runs it through log_adapters.parse_line, and writes a unified record into agentvision/actions.jsonl, where the jsonl adapter covers every JSON logger in one go (its field-alias sets accept ts/time/timestamp/@timestamp, level/lvl/severity, message/msg/event, and both the pino 10-60 and syslog 0-7 numeric level scales, so slog, zerolog, zap and tracing-json all normalise without a custom adapter). No rebuild, no code change, no config file. FOUR THINGS THIS PATH DOES THAT YOU MUST KNOW. (1) The record's ts/ts_ms are the WRAPPER'S ARRIVAL TIME, deliberately — that is the same clock frames are stamped with — and the line's own timestamp is preserved only as data.emit_ts_ms. Any correlation you do is against arrival, so a buffered writer or a busy pipe skews it. (2) The tee LOCKS the first strong adapter (anything but raw/generic_ts) for the rest of the run and then forces it per line. On a mixed stream — JSON on stdout, a panic or a Go runtime traceback on stderr — the locked jsonl adapter returns None for those lines and parse_line falls back to `raw`, so they land with level="" and category "log". (3) Consequence of (2), and it is the important one: a Rust `thread 'main' panicked at ...` or a Go `fatal error: all goroutines are asleep` is NOT a failure trigger. _detect_failure_records wants category error/exception/fatal, level ERROR/FATAL/CRITICAL, or a failure word in `source`; and content escalation only matches value-shaped failures (ok=false, failed=true, status=5xx, non-zero exit/error counts, "failed to", "timed out", refused/unreachable) — "panicked at" matches none of them. So the loudest thing your binary can print will sit in the log as an ordinary row. Fix it explicitly: av_watch(regex="panicked at|^goroutine \\d+|fatal error:|SIGSEGV") at minimum, or write the adapter with av_add_adapter and pin it. (4) ENFORCEMENT: go and rust are in _ONE_ARTIFACT_LANGS, so this id is recorded intent — and it only takes effect at all if the program is actually launched through `agentvision run`. Selecting run_wrapper and then starting the binary from systemd bridges nothing. THE OTHER BRANCH, PREFERRED WHEN IT APPLIES: if the JSON already goes to a FILE inside the project, do not install anything — emitters:[] with adapters={"<stem>":"auto"} and a rationale containing "already". That is the cleanest bridge in this whole set: no wrapper, no relaunch, the program's own timestamps survive intact (read at the source rather than re-stamped on arrival), and no adapter lock-in.
recipes.deliberately_not: stdout_tee — its own catalog entry says so: "for a COMPILED program use run_wrapper instead: there is no in-process hook to install in a native binary", and its `languages` field is interpreted languages loaded in-process. On go/rust it is recorded-only anyway. Selecting both is naming the same tee twice and eats the two-id budget. lifecycle — cli.py already writes av.wrapper.start (argv, project, pid) and av.wrapper.exit with the real exit_code around the child, so the run_wrapper selection includes the lifecycle facet; the catalog states outright that for compiled programs "the run_wrapper reports the exit code, so selecting both is not additive". Nothing else on go/rust emits lifecycle at all. A SIDE EFFECT TO EXPECT rather than a warning: on Go, installer.py writes agentvision/emitters/av_emit.go — a real `package emitters` source file inside your module that `go build ./...` and `go vet ./...` will compile (stdlib only, nothing imports it). On Rust it writes only RUST_README.txt; on C/C++ only CPP_README.txt.
recipes.adapters: This is the shape where adapter WORK, not emitter work, is the job — and where av_test_adapter should run BEFORE you commit, not after. Take a real line from the existing JSON log (or from one manual run of the binary) and call av_test_adapter(line=<that line>). Check three things in the reply: is_fallback is false, `level` matches what the line says, and `source` is your program's own module/component and NOT the adapter's name or "structural". "auto" is usually the correct value to write down — but only once you have SEEN what auto picks. TWO SPECIFIC MISPARSES TO LOOK FOR IN THE REPLY. (a) The jsonl adapter consumes the FIRST match from its source-key list — source, logger, name, module, logger_name, caller, category, SourceContext, c, ctx, SYSLOG_IDENTIFIER, _SYSTEMD_UNIT, host, channel — so a zerolog field you added called `host` or `channel` or `c` silently becomes the event's `source`, and av_errors_by_fingerprint then groups by it. (b) Numeric levels are mapped by scale (>=10 as pino 10-60, else syslog 0-7), so a custom integer severity of your own invention comes out as a wrong word rather than as an error. If the format is genuinely uncovered — the catalog reports covered:false for a discovered source when only a fallback claimed its sampled lines — you MUST either write an adapter with av_add_adapter (real sample line, structural anchor tokens, and the also_match lines are enforced) and pin it, or say in plan.rationale that you accept the weaker parse. Sealing with neither is rejected at commit, which is the correct outcome: a fallback keeps every call succeeding while flattening `source` to the fallback's own name.
recipes.visual_capture: FALSE for a service or CLI — and this is the one recipe here where the answer flips on a sub-case, so decide rather than default. A headless Go/Rust binary has no window; frames are pure waste and every frames_on_disk tool is inert. BUT if it is a full-screen TUI (bubbletea, ratatui, crossterm, ncurses), the tee is close to useless on its own — the UI is redrawn with ANSI escape sequences and carriage returns, which land as line noise in the sink — and a screenshot of the terminal window plus av_ocr_frame or av_read_screen may be the only readable view of what the user actually saw. That makes visual_capture=true defensible for a TUI and only for a TUI. Say which sub-case you are in, in the rationale.
recipes.what_would_still_be_invisible: 1) ANYTHING NOT PRINTED — and in compiled languages that is a large set. A goroutine deadlock prints nothing until the runtime detects a total deadlock; a Rust build with panic=abort leaves only the exit status; a segfault or a Go `SIGSEGV` in cgo can kill the process mid-line. run_wrapper's own catalog entry states it: "a segfault leaves only the exit status, and output buffered at crash time can be lost entirely". That last part is literal — a JSON logger with a buffered writer loses whatever had not flushed. 2) THE PROGRAM'S OWN TIMESTAMPS, as the timeline's basis. They survive as data.emit_ts_ms but the canonical ts is arrival; if you need exact intra-run timing, read the file directly with the pin branch instead of teeing. 3) PANICS AS FAILURES — until you add the watch or the adapter described above. This is worth re-stating because it inverts the usual expectation: the JSON INFO lines classify correctly and the fatal crash does not. 4) METRICS AND TRACES. A /metrics endpoint, an OTLP exporter, or pprof output is not a log line and nothing here scrapes any of them. Structured fields inside the JSON DO survive (unconsumed keys land in data.*), so a field you add is usually the cheapest way to make something visible. 5) A BINARY LAUNCHED WITHOUT THE WRAPPER. run_wrapper is intent only; systemd/Docker/`./app &` bypasses it and the bridge stays empty while reporting BUILT. av_log_where is the check that catches this — it asks the OS which descriptors the process actually holds, including stdout going to a terminal, a pipe, or /dev/null, which no configured path can reveal. 6) av_install_verify cannot help you here: for go/rust it returns mode="static" and only confirms the emitter files exist and the sink is writable.

recipes.shape: An Electron or hybrid desktop/web app with BOTH layers: a Node main process and a Chromium renderer running the actual UI. Two runtimes, two failure surfaces, and the one users see (the renderer) is the one the server-side emitter mechanism physically cannot reach. This is the only shape in this set that needs an emitter AgentVision offers but does not install.
how_to_recognise: MANIFEST: package.json with "main": "main.js"/"electron.js" and electron in devDependencies; electron-builder / forge.config.js / electron.vite.config.ts; a "build" section with appId. detect_language -> "node" (package.json is the marker), so the catalog offers five ids: stdout_tee, lifecycle, uncaught_exceptions, logging_bridge, browser_events — reject at 3, so at most 2.

TWO-LAYER STRUCTURE, by file: main.js / src/main/index.ts using `BrowserWindow`, `app.whenReady()`, `ipcMain`; a preload.js using contextBridge/ipcRenderer; a renderer/ or src/renderer/ dir with index.html plus a bundler config (vite.config.ts, webpack.config.js) and React/Vue/Svelte components. tsconfig.json alongside.

CODE EVIDENCE: `gui_toolkit` will fire on "electron" itself; expect `async` and `network_io` (fetch/axios) high, `threads` low, `web_service` maybe present if it also runs a local server. gui_toolkit matching electron + a package.json main field is the fingerprint — it separates this from a plain Node service (no BrowserWindow, no renderer dir) and from a pure browser SPA (no main process).

Confirm the split before planning: if there is no renderer/index.html at all it is a Node service, and browser_events is wrong. If there is no Node main process it is a plain web front end, and the renderer half below is the WHOLE recipe.
recipes.why_each: browser_events, because the renderer is where the user-visible failure lives and it is the ONLY emitter that sees the client half. agent_bootstrap/av_browser.js captures window.onerror, unhandledrejection (on a modern app the most common real failure), console.error/warn, non-2xx and THROWN fetch/XHR (CORS, DNS, offline — a class the server never sees at all), securitypolicyviolation, and resource load errors, each with the throwing module/line pulled out of the stack. The Node emitter cannot substitute: its mechanism is NODE_OPTIONS=--require, a server-side hook that cannot load in a page context. uncaught_exceptions, because the main process still owns the window lifecycle, the file system and IPC, and av_emit.js installs process.on('uncaughtException') and process.on('unhandledRejection') — preserving default crash behaviour by re-exiting only when it is the sole listener. Between them you cover the two runtimes with two ids. NOW THE PART THAT DECIDES WHETHER THIS RECIPE WORKS AT ALL. browser_events BUILDS NOTHING. emitters.build_emitter("node") returns files={emitters/av_emit.js}, installer.py writes exactly spec.files, and nothing anywhere in the tree copies agent_bootstrap/av_browser.js into a project — the only references to that filename are the catalog's own `builds_as` text and its tests. emitters.selection_report() will tell you as much: for browser_events on node it returns enforced:false, "this id maps to no runtime hook in this build, so selecting it changes nothing". So you must place it yourself: copy <AGENTVISION_ROOT>/agent_bootstrap/av_browser.js into the renderer's served assets (or `import` it first in the renderer entry) and load it with data-av-endpoint="http://127.0.0.1:7771/browser/ingest" (7771 is bridge_server's default port). The page POSTs batched NDJSON to /browser/ingest, which appends to <project_root>/agentvision/log.txt — the "text" sink — and requires the ACTIVE profile to have a project_root (else 409 NO_PROJECT_ROOT) and every record to carry av:"browser" (else it is counted as missing_av_browser_marker and dropped). ENFORCEMENT on node is weaker than the report claims: build_emitter puts AGENTVISION_HOOKS into run_env for python ONLY, and av_emit.js contains no AGENTVISION_HOOKS check, so console.*, the exception handlers and the lifecycle records are ALL always on once it loads. selection_report says enforced:true for hook ids on node; the spec's own selection_enforced is false. The two fields sit in the same install report and disagree — believe the emitter file.
recipes.deliberately_not: stdout_tee — on node this is console.* patching, not the stdout stream, and av_emit.js does that whether or not you select it. Selecting it records coverage of "stdout" that you do not have: a native module or a child process writing to fd 1 directly is invisible to console patching. logging_bridge — the node menu offers it, but av_emit.js contains NO logging-framework hook of any kind: no winston transport, no pino destination. Selecting it changes nothing and would make the plan claim the app's logger is routed when it is not (if the app uses winston/pino, add a file transport pointed at process.env.AGENTVISION_SINK yourself — that is a code change, not an emitter). lifecycle — av_emit.js always emits av.node.start (pid, argv, node version, cwd) and av.node.exit (with the exit code, unlike the python hook), ungated. Selecting it is a no-op record and spends a slot. A DUPLICATION TO EXPECT, not a reason to change the plan: cli.py's _child_has_inprocess_emitter keys on the executable BASENAME and only suppresses the wrapper's own tee for python/node/ruby. Launch as `agentvision run -- npx electron .` and argv[0] is "electron" or "npx", so the wrapper ALSO tees and adapter-parses every stdout line on top of av_emit.js's records — two records per console line (av.node.console.* and av.wrapper.stdout). Know it so you do not read it as the app logging twice.
recipes.adapters: Two sinks and two DIFFERENT formats, which is unique to this shape. events -> jsonl carries av_emit.js's native records (fine, the installer pins it). text -> auto must resolve to browser_av_json for the ingested browser lines — connectors/adapters/browser.py registers it before `jsonl` precisely because jsonl would otherwise claim those lines at 1.0 and flatten the browser-specific fields (source_file, source_line, status, blocked_url, repeat). The /browser/ingest response even tells you the intended adapter: "browser_av_json". VERIFY IT, because auto-detection samples up to 60 lines of log.txt and that file can also receive av_runtime-style text lines if any python part of the project is bridged: call av_test_adapter(line=<a real ingested line>) and check is_fallback=false and that `source` is the throwing module (e.g. "Cart.tsx") rather than "structural" or the adapter's own name. If it resolves wrongly, pin adapters={"text":"browser_av_json"} explicitly — a valid label whose value is not a registered adapter is rejected at commit, so a typo cannot slip through, but a silently WRONG auto-detection can.
recipes.visual_capture: TRUE, but for a narrower reason than shape 2 — say the reason, because the tempting justification is the wrong one. The renderer already reports its own errors as structured events WITH file and line, so frames are not how you find a TypeError. Frames earn their place for the failures that produce no error at all: a white screen after a bundle failed to load, a modal rendered off-screen, a layout that collapses at a window size, an update that silently did not repaint. Pair them with the browser emitter's own resource_error and CSP records — those two together distinguish "the asset 404'd" from "the asset loaded and the component rendered nothing". Ask the user for the interval (1s is plenty for a layout bug; 0.2s if the complaint is a flash or a transition). Treat av_ui_tree as unverified here rather than assumed: Chromium exposes an accessibility tree to the OS only under some conditions, and the tool's `needs` are accessibility_api + gui_program — test it once on this app and record the answer instead of planning around it.
recipes.what_would_still_be_invisible: 1) THE EMITTER'S OWN SILENCE — check this FIRST, before believing any empty result. av_browser.js's safety rule 2 is "never log its own failures", so its transport fetch ends in .catch(silent): if the renderer's CSP blocks connect-src to 127.0.0.1:7771, or the bridge is not running, or the profile has no project_root, the page looks fully instrumented and the sink stays empty forever. The positive proof is the announcement record it pushes on load — search the text sink for "browser emitter armed (session=...)" with its captures list. No armed record means nothing else from that page is trustworthy either. 2) EVERY OTHER PAGE CONTEXT. The emitter's own `misses` says it: anything before the script loads, anything in a different tab, anything in a web worker. In Electron that means a SECOND BrowserWindow, a webview/iframe, and any worker each need their own copy loaded — one instance covers one page context. Preload/isolated-world code is not covered by a script tag in the page context. 3) IPC. Neither emitter records ipcMain/ipcRenderer traffic, so "the renderer asked for X and the main process never answered" is invisible on both sides — the classic Electron hang, and the one you will most want. Instrument it yourself: av_emit.js exposes global.__agentvisionEmit(category, source, data) for exactly this, and av_browser.js has no equivalent public hook. 4) NATIVE-LAYER CRASHES. A Chromium renderer or GPU-process crash runs no JS, so nothing emits; you get the wrapper's exit code if you launched through it, and a blank frame. Same for a native module segfault. 5) console.log. The browser emitter deliberately excludes it (volume, no signal) while the NODE emitter captures all five console methods — so the same call is recorded in the main process and dropped in the renderer. That asymmetry will look like missing data if you do not expect it. 6) WHETHER ELECTRON LOADED av_emit.js AT ALL. av_install_verify's node probe spawns plain `node -e` with NODE_OPTIONS=--require: a pass proves the emitter file works under Node, NOT that Electron honoured NODE_OPTIONS for its main process (packaged builds and Electron's own flag filtering are separate questions). The real check is an av.node.start record in agentvision/actions.jsonl with the argv of your actual app.

recipes.shape: 1. Browser single-page app (React/Vue/Svelte) served by a dev server
how_to_recognise: package.json with react/vue/svelte in dependencies AND a dev script running vite / next dev / webpack serve / ng serve; an index.html containing <div id="root"> or <div id="app">; vite.config.*, svelte.config.js, next.config.*.

detect_language() returns "node" for ANY project with package.json or tsconfig.json (connectors/log_sources.py:464). browser_events is only offered for node/javascript/typescript/ts/js (bridge_plan.py:135). If emitters_available has no browser_events, the profile's language is wrong — fix it before planning, because the node emitter's mechanism is NODE_OPTIONS=--require, which can never load in a page.

EXPECT code_evidence TO BE NEARLY EMPTY, AND DO NOT READ THAT AS 'NOTHING NEEDED'. bridge_plan._EXT_LANG (line ~274) lists .js/.mjs/.ts but NOT .tsx/.jsx/.vue/.svelte, so a modern SPA's components are never scanned at all; code_signals also caps at 400 files and skips node_modules/dist/build. Read the target yourself: av_codebase_map, then av_source_search for 'createRoot|createApp|mount(', 'fetch(|axios', 'useEffect|onMounted'.
Note the dev-server origin/port: the page must be able to POST to the bridge (127.0.0.1:7771 by default), or set data-av-endpoint on the script tag.
node's menu is 5 ids, so blanket_threshold makes the cap 3 emitters (bridge_plan.blanket_threshold). One is the right answer here.
recipes.why_each: browser_events is the ONLY emitter in the entire catalog that can see the half of this program where its user-visible failures happen. agent_bootstrap/av_browser.js captures window.onerror, unhandledrejection (on a modern app the most common real failure), console.error/warn, fetch/XHR non-2xx AND thrown fetch (CORS/DNS/offline — the server has no record of that class at all), securitypolicyviolation, and resource load errors. Tie the justification to network_io/async if code_evidence found them; if code_evidence is empty because of the .tsx blind spot above, say that in plan.why and cite the imports you grepped instead — a reason that names a signal you did not actually observe is worse than one that names the blind spot. BE HONEST ABOUT WHAT COMMITTING THIS DOES: selection_report() correctly reports browser_events as enforced=false, 'maps to no runtime hook'. It installs NO FILE — nothing in the tree copies av_browser.js into a project (grep: only bridge_plan.py mentions the path), while build_emitter('node') writes agentvision/emitters/av_emit.js, which you did NOT select. You must copy <AGENTVISION_ROOT>/agent_bootstrap/av_browser.js into a served static dir yourself (Vite: public/agentvision/av_browser.js) and add <script src="/agentvision/av_browser.js" data-av-endpoint="http://127.0.0.1:7771/browser/ingest"> (or import it first in the entry module), dev builds only. Confirm it armed: the emitter's first record is 'browser emitter armed (session=…)' with the captures list.
recipes.deliberately_not: stdout_tee, logging_bridge, uncaught_exceptions — all three are facets of av_emit.js, a SERVER-side --require hook that cannot load in a browser; selecting them would record intent for a program half that is not where this app fails. logging_bridge is doubly empty on node: av_emit.js contains no logging-framework hook at all. Also NOT selecting the dev server's own stdout as an emitter: for node the wrapper tee is not an offered id (run_wrapper is only offered for go/rust/cpp/c/shell/unknown), so bridge the dev server out of band by launching it as `agentvision run -- npm run dev` and say so in rationale. That works because _child_has_inprocess_emitter keys on the literal exe name (cli.py:352-359): 'npm' is not node/nodejs, so the tee emits JSONL — MEASURED with the same rule using `sh -c "node app.js"`, which teed every line and duplicated console lines (av.node.console.info AND av.wrapper.stdout).
recipes.adapters: Browser records do NOT land in actions.jsonl. POST /browser/ingest appends them to <project_root>/agentvision/log.txt (bridge_server.py:4496-4584), i.e. the TEXT sink. Pin that label to "auto" — and use the label exactly as it appears in catalog.adapter_pin_labels (an installed project's profile calls it 'textlog'; the catalog default set is {'events','text'}; a wrong key is REJECTED, not silently ignored). Verify first, as the catalog demands: MEASURED today, a real browser record classifies as browser_av_json at 1.00 with level=ERROR and source=Cart.tsx — the throwing module, which is exactly the source field you want. Do not pin 'jsonl': it also scores 1.00 and would flatten the browser-specific fields (browser_av_json is deliberately registered first). Ingest facts worth knowing: 409 NO_PROJECT_ROOT if the active profile has no project_root; every record must carry av:"browser" or it is rejected and counted; caps are 500 records/POST, 8000 bytes/record, 2 MB/body; and it always appends to the ACTIVE profile's sink — switch profiles mid-session and your page's errors go into another program's log.
recipes.visual_capture: FALSE by default, and say why: browser_events already carries the error, the stack, the module and the failing URL, and frames of a browser window cost real disk. Flip it to TRUE only for the one failure this emitter is blind to — 'it renders wrong but throws nothing'. Then set capture_app to the browser app name, accept that you are capturing the WHOLE browser window (tabs, devtools, other pages), and ASK the user for the interval (a mostly-static page is fine at 1-2 s). av_ui_tree/av_ui_diff are a trap here: they need accessibility_api + gui_program and return the browser's chrome, not your component tree.
recipes.what_would_still_be_invisible: Everything before the script executes — a bundle parse error, an SSR 500, index.html itself failing to load. Anything in a web worker, iframe, service worker, or a second tab (each document needs its own script tag). console.log, all successful requests, and request/response bodies (deliberately dropped: volume and user data). A React error boundary that catches and renders a fallback: it never reaches window.onerror, so all you get is console.error IF the framework logs it. A wrong VALUE rendered with no error — no state emitter exists for the page. Events beyond the 200-item queue or past the 50-signature dedupe cap (you do get a 'N event(s) dropped' WARN, so the loss is at least visible). Anything queued when the tab is hard-killed (visibilitychange/pagehide flush via sendBeacon; a crashed tab loses the tail). And the entire server half unless you separately launch the dev server through the wrapper. Finally, av_install_verify cannot prove any of this: for node it probes av_emit.js with `node -e`, never av_browser.js.

recipes.shape: 2. Plain-Python utility that reads keypresses / automates input
how_to_recognise: A handful of .py files, maybe requirements.txt, no framework markers. The decisive evidence is the IMPORTS, and you must grep for them yourself: tty+termios+select, curses, msvcrt, readchar/getch, pynput (keyboard.Listener/mouse.Listener), keyboard, sshkeyboard, evdev, pygame.event — or on the injection side pyautogui, pydirectinput, cliclick, osascript, robotjs.
Concrete greps: 'termios', 'tcsetattr', 'sys.stdin.read(1)', 'getch', 'pynput', 'keyboard.Listener', 'pyautogui', 'SendInput'.

code_evidence IS BLIND TO THIS SHAPE — this is the gap the owner found. _CODE_SIGNALS has no input-capture pattern at all; its gui_toolkit list is tkinter/PyQt/PySide/kivy/wx/Avalonia/WinForms/electron/SwiftUI/Cocoa/GLFW/SDL/imgui only. A keypress utility looks identical to any other small script: you will typically see only prints_only, and threads if it uses pynput (whose Listener IS a thread).
Split the shape before choosing, because the two halves get different answers: (a) it READS the human's keys; (b) it INJECTS keys/clicks into other apps.
recipes.why_each: stdout_tee: on python the selection is genuinely enforced (installer bakes AGENTVISION_HOOKS into <project>/sitecustomize.py; av_runtime._selected_hooks gates each hook), and for a keypress reader the line the program PRINTS is the only in-process evidence of what it decoded — that is the prints_only signal, and it is cheap. Know its shape: records are category stdout/stderr with data.text and NO level (MEASURED: 'ERROR:root:boom' arrived as category=stderr, level=None). uncaught_exceptions: select it for its threading.excepthook half, not the main hook — a pynput/keyboard listener thread that raises reaches neither sys.excepthook nor stderr in any useful form (threads signal); it also covers the classic 'died before tcsetattr restore, terminal left in raw mode' exit, via the unraisable/shutdown hook. Enforcement caveat that applies to both: `agentvision run` prepends <AV_ROOT>/agent_bootstrap to PYTHONPATH, and THAT sitecustomize sets no AGENTVISION_HOOKS, so all five hooks arm regardless of your plan — read data.hooks_selection_source in the start record ('plan' vs 'default (all)') instead of assuming. If the project already had its own sitecustomize.py the installer leaves it untouched and your selection is written nowhere at all.
recipes.deliberately_not: logging_bridge — MEASURED COST, and it is a behaviour change, not just noise: FIXED - this WAS true and is no longer: AgentVision's handler is attached to root at interpreter start, which made a later logging.basicConfig() a no-op (basicConfig only acts when root has no handlers), so a script that normally printed WARNING/ERROR printed NOTHING while the records were still captured to JSONL. av_runtime._shield_basicconfig now hides our handler for the duration of that call, so the program configures the root it expects and its console output is unchanged. Verified by agent_bootstrap/test_av_runtime_hooks.py. What remains is smaller: with a bare basicConfig() the root level is raised WARNING->INFO so INFO reaches the program's own handlers too; an EXPLICIT level= is respected untouched. For an interactive tool whose console IS the interface, do not do that; and a small utility usually has no logging to route anyway. swallowed_exceptions — only if discards_error is present IN STRENGTH; two excepts in a 50-line script is evidence of almost nothing, and on <3.12 it silently never arms (compare hooks_requested vs hooks_armed, and catches_swallowed_exceptions in the start record). UPDATE - THIS GAP IS NOW CLOSED: `user_input` IS a selectable emitter id. Selecting it sets capture_user_input=true on the profile via the install report's profile_overrides. It still needs the daemon running (`agentvision daemon start`), and it still fails CLOSED and counts drops, so check av_daemon_status() before reading an empty input log as 'no input'. Add it to this shape's emitter set when the question is whether the keypress ARRIVED at all. python_backend/daemon/input_daemon.py records physical keyboard/mouse, but it is reachable only out of band: (1) set capture_user_input on the profile — POST /profiles REPLACES the profile from the dict you send (bridge_server ~4595; ProgramProfile.from_dict drops unknown keys), so read it first with av_active_profile and re-post it WHOLE with capture_user_input:true, or you will wipe log paths and crop settings; (2) start the daemon — there is NO HTTP or MCP start route: the GUI Permissions tab, `python -m python_backend.cli daemon start`, or `agentvision run --record-input` (starts it detached); (3) confirm with av_daemon_status (running, pid, which sink, capture_user_input). macOS needs Accessibility or CGEventTapCreate fails outright (exit 3). For sub-shape (b) you need NO opt-in: synthetic/injected events are always recorded. Record all of this in plan.rationale, because the plan schema has nowhere else to put it.
recipes.adapters: Usually nothing to pin: both av_runtime and the daemon write the unified schema, and MEASURED, jsonl claims a real record at 1.00 and preserves the record's own source. What matters far more here is SINK IDENTITY: av_runtime writes to AGENTVISION_LOG_DIR/actions.jsonl (under `agentvision run` that is <project>/agentvision/actions.jsonl; with a bare interpreter and no env var it is <project>/log/actions.jsonl — that is where my probe landed), while the input daemon writes the PROFILE's action_log_file. Prove they are the same file with av_log_sources plus av_log_where (POSIX only — it is pure lsof and returns available:false on Windows), or you will read one file and be blind to the other. Daemon record shape to expect: category key/mouse; source av.daemon.key.press|release|modifier and av.daemon.mouse.click|move|scroll; data.keycode is the RAW OS keycode (mac CGKeyCode / Windows VK / evdev code — no character translation, no modifier folding); data.kind physical|synthetic; source_pid 0 for physical, the real injector pid on macOS, -1 on Windows/Linux; coords on mouse events; moves coalesced to one per 100 ms; frame_seq ALWAYS null. If the utility keeps its own text log, av_test_adapter a real line first — see recipe 4 for how confidently wrong that can go.
recipes.visual_capture: Sub-shape (a), a terminal keypress reader: FALSE — no gui_toolkit signal, the keys are already structured in the JSONL, and OCRing a terminal needs an installed OCR backend for little gain. Sub-shape (b), an automation utility driving other apps: TRUE, and it is the entire point — the daemon's synthetic events carry coords{x,y} but frame_seq is null, so the ONLY way to see what a click actually landed on is frames aligned by timestamp (av_actions_around_frame, av_frame_region). Ask the user for the interval; injection is fast, so 0.2-0.5 s beats 1 s, and watch av_retention because that rate fills disk.
recipes.what_would_still_be_invisible: WHICH KEY THE PROGRAM ACTUALLY RECEIVED. The daemon taps the OS, not your process's read: a key eaten by another focused app, or swallowed by the terminal, produces an identical record. Characters and text (raw keycodes only). Which application was focused — there is no window/app attribution anywhere in the daemon records. On Linux, X11 XTEST and Wayland virtual-pointer injection are invisible entirely (they bypass /dev/input), and the injector pid is never known. The terminal's own state (raw mode on/off, echo). And a measured trap that can BECOME the bug you chase: `agentvision run` spawns the child with stdout=PIPE and stderr=PIPE (cli.py:617-620) and leaves stdin alone, so stdout.isatty() is False while stdin is still the tty — curses, Rich, colour and spinner paths change behaviour or refuse under the wrapper. Also add --no-watch-files unless file writes are your subject: MEASURED, a 5-second run that printed one line produced 11 records, 6 of them the wrapper's own file-watcher noise about AgentVision's own sink (5 × file.modify agentvision/actions.jsonl, one per second — the ignore list has 'log' but not 'agentvision').

recipes.shape: 3. Python REST service (Flask/FastAPI) behind gunicorn or uvicorn
how_to_recognise: requirements.txt / pyproject with flask|fastapi|starlette + gunicorn|uvicorn; an app object (app = FastAPI() / Flask(__name__)); routers under app/api/*.py; no GUI imports.

The launch line is part of the recognition, not a detail: Procfile, Dockerfile CMD, systemd unit or Makefile target naming `gunicorn -w N app:app` or `uvicorn app:app --workers N --reload`. The worker count and the reloader decide whether your hooks will be alive at all (see why_each).
code_evidence should show web_service (flask|django|fastapi|…), plus async (async def/await) and network_io (httpx/requests). web_service is also the catalog's own argument for visual_capture:false.

Check existing_logs_found: a service usually already writes something (logs/app.log, gunicorn error log). Each undeclared entry carries a coverage verdict, and an entry NO adapter specifically parses will block the commit unless you pin one or state that you accept the weaker parse.
recipes.why_each: A framework service almost never lets an exception reach sys.excepthook — it catches per request and LOGS it. That makes the logging call, not the crash, the carrier of failure (existing_logging + logs_in_handler signals), and logging_bridge is the only emitter that captures it as structure: MEASURED, records arrive as category log/warn/error with source av.bootstrap.log.<logger>, data.level exact (INFO/WARNING/ERROR), plus logger, module, func and line. STATE THE COST BEFORE COMMITTING, because it is measured and it changes the program: the handler is attached at interpreter start, so a later logging.basicConfig() is a no-op and console logging can disappear (a script printing 'WARNING warn-line' printed nothing with the bridge armed), and av_runtime raises root from WARNING to INFO, so any handler the app adds afterwards starts receiving INFO records it never saw before. On a service with its own dictConfig the usual outcome is extra console INFO rather than silence — verify on the real service instead of assuming either way. THE THING THAT WILL SILENTLY BREAK THIS PLAN, MEASURED TODAY: install_all_hooks is guarded by the ENV var AGENTVISION_HOOKED, which av_runtime sets into os.environ, so every child inherits it. A multiprocessing SPAWN child produced ZERO records — its logging.error and its print were completely absent (4 records total, none from the worker). A FORK child DID emit, but under the PARENT's run_id, and no log record carries a pid at all, so worker attribution is impossible. Clearing AGENTVISION_HOOKED before spawning made the spawned child hook normally, which proves the guard is the cause. So: gunicorn's pre-fork workers emit but are indistinguishable from each other; anything that starts workers through a FRESH interpreter (spawn-based multiprocessing, a re-exec'ing reloader) emits nothing. VERIFY, do not assume — count av.bootstrap.start records against your worker count (av_search source="av.bootstrap.start") and read data.hooks_selection_source ('plan' = your selection gated it; 'default (all)' = the `agentvision run` bootstrap armed all five because <AV_ROOT>/agent_bootstrap/sitecustomize sets no AGENTVISION_HOOKS). Also: N workers append to ONE actions.jsonl and av_runtime's lock is a per-process threading.Lock, so long records (tracebacks) from concurrent workers can interleave. LAUNCHER CHOICE: `agentvision run -- gunicorn app:app` has exe 'gunicorn', and _child_has_inprocess_emitter only recognises exe names starting with 'python' (cli.py:345-359), so the wrapper tee ALSO writes a JSONL record per stdout/stderr line on top of the in-process hooks — MEASURED that exact rule on node (exe 'sh' → every line teed AND console lines duplicated). Prefer `agentvision run -- python -m gunicorn app:app`, and pass --no-watch-files (measured: 6 of 11 records in a 5 s run were the watcher's own noise about AgentVision's sink).
recipes.deliberately_not: uncaught_exceptions — the tempting-but-wrong pick for this shape. The framework's error middleware catches request exceptions, so the excepthook rarely fires; you would be recording an expectation the program never satisfies. stdout_tee — with logging_bridge armed and any stream handler configured you get every event twice (once structured, once as raw text), plus gunicorn/uvicorn access prose you do not want on the timeline. swallowed_exceptions — only when discards_error is high AND the service runs 3.12+; it is scoped to project files and deduped (which is right), but on a busy service it is still volume, and on <3.12 it never arms while still appearing in hooks_requested.
recipes.adapters: Pin the JSONL events label to auto/jsonl (MEASURED jsonl 1.00, and it preserves source av.bootstrap.log.<logger>) and deliberately do NOT plan to read the server's console prose. Measured on real-shaped lines: a uvicorn access line — 'INFO:     127.0.0.1:52341 - "GET /api/items HTTP/1.1" 500 Internal Server Error' — is claimed by jul_2line at 0.85 with level=INFO and source='jul'. A 500 filed as INFO, under a Java-logging source name, and is_fallback is FALSE because only structural/generic_ts/raw count as fallback (log_sources.py:663), so nothing warns you. gunicorn's own error line → gunicorn_error 1.00, ERROR, source gunicorn (good). Flask's dev access line → dev_access 1.00, level ERROR, source 127.0.0.1 (good). A python-logging TEXT line → python_logging 1.00 but source comes back as 'python_logging' — the adapter's own name, not myapp.views — which is exactly failure mode (3) the catalog tells you to check for, and it breaks av_errors_by_fingerprint grouping and av_source_at_error. That is the strongest argument for taking the structured JSONL instead of parsing text. If you must read an access log, av_add_adapter one for it and pin it under its label; if you accept the weaker parse, say so in rationale or the commit gate will refuse.
recipes.visual_capture: FALSE, explicitly and on the web_service signal — there is no window. That also makes every frame tool irrelevant and worth naming in tools.not_relevant: av_get_frame, av_frame_json/region/overlay, av_read_screen, av_ocr_frame, av_visual_changes/events, av_ui_tree/av_ui_diff, av_diff, av_replay, av_token_report, av_frames_awaiting. av_wait_for is still fine with condition='log' or 'error_fingerprint'; only its 'frame' branch needs capture.
recipes.what_would_still_be_invisible: WHICH REQUEST caused it — av_runtime always writes trace_id null, and a logging record carries logger/module/func/line but nothing about method, path, status or a request id. Which worker or pid (no pid field in log records; shared run_id under fork; nothing at all from a spawned worker — measured). A 4xx/5xx the framework returns WITHOUT logging: a Flask abort(404) or a FastAPI HTTPException produces no log call, therefore no record — your bridge will show a healthy service while clients get errors. Request/response bodies and headers, DB queries, and all latency/throughput: there is no metric emitter anywhere in this catalog (av_metrics reports the CAPTURE process's cpu/rss over frames, not your handler timings). Anything logged by a process whose interpreter never loaded the bootstrap (a reloader supervisor, a helper launched with a scrubbed env). And the health of the sink itself under concurrency — interleaved partial lines would read as unparseable records, so if av_log_raw shows JSON fragments, suspect multi-worker appends before you suspect the parser.

recipes.shape: 4. Compiled C/C++ game or emulator with its own printf logging
how_to_recognise: CMakeLists.txt / meson.build / *.vcxproj / conanfile / Makefile alongside .c/.cpp/.h. detect_language returns 'cpp' — plain C reports 'cpp' too (both the markers at log_sources.py:473 and the extension census map .c/.h to cpp); that is expected, not a misdetection.

code_evidence IS meaningful for this shape (bridge_plan._EXT_LANG covers .c/.cc/.cpp/.h). Expect gui_toolkit (SDL|GLFW|imgui) — the catalog's own argument for visual_capture:true — plus threads (std::thread) and file_io.

Do NOT expect prints_only to fire for C: its regex matches print(/puts/echo only, so printf/fprintf/std::cout never trip it. Read the source for the log macro yourself (av_source_search for 'printf|fprintf|std::cout|LOG(|spdlog|SDL_Log') and grab a few REAL output lines — you need them for the adapter check below.
Check existing_logs_found for the game's own log file (undeclared entries are labelled by file stem, e.g. 'emulator' for logs/emulator.log) and read its coverage verdict.
cpp is offered only 3 ids, so blanket_threshold caps you at 2. One is the honest answer.
recipes.why_each: There is no in-process hook to install in a native binary, and the catalog says so in stdout_tee's own note. run_wrapper is `agentvision run -- ./yourapp`: stdout/stderr teed, normalized through the adapters into agentvision/actions.jsonl, plus the exit code. The evidence-tied reason is that this program's diagnostics ALREADY EXIST as its printf stream (and its own log file) — the job is to capture and time-align them, not to inject logging. Say plainly in the plan that this is RECORDED, not enforced: selection_report() returns enforced=false with 'builds ONE artifact' for cpp (emitters._ONE_ARTIFACT_LANGS), the artifact is agentvision/emitters/CPP_README.txt plus the tee, and nothing whatsoever is compiled into your binary. It only takes effect when the program is actually launched through the wrapper — a run started from an IDE or a shell alias emits nothing.
recipes.deliberately_not: stdout_tee — the catalog's own note routes compiled programs to run_wrapper, and on cpp both ids are facets of the same single artifact, so selecting both records two decisions and builds one. lifecycle — explicitly NOT additive here: its builds_as says the run_wrapper already reports the exit code, so adding it buys nothing and eats your 2-id budget. Nothing else is even offered for cpp (no in-process hooks, no config drop-in), which is worth stating in rationale so a later session does not wonder whether swallowed_exceptions was forgotten: it does not exist for this language.
recipes.adapters: This is where a C/C++ bridge actually goes wrong, and the tee makes it worse in a way pins cannot fix. _emit_console_line auto-detects per line ONLY until the first STRONG match, then LOCKS that adapter for the rest of the run (cli.py:288-292), and it writes the resolved category/level/source INTO the sink — so a wrong pick is frozen in the stored data, and plan.adapters (which governs how a source is READ) cannot undo it. MEASURED today on real-shaped lines: '[DEBUG] Sprite.c:32 - loaded 4 tiles' → coreboot_cbmem at 1.00 with source='coreboot' (the documented trap, reproduced); 'Loading level 3... done (42 ms)' → openplc_runtime at 0.80 with source='openplc'; a spdlog line '[2026-07-30 10:12:01.123] [render] [error] shader compile failed' → spdlog 1.00 with source='render' (correct — the program's own subsystem). None of the wrong ones set is_fallback, because only structural/generic_ts/raw do. So the procedure is: do a SHORT run first, take the first few real lines, av_test_adapter each one, and check is_fallback + level + source. If a wrong adapter claims them, av_add_adapter one for this program's format and pin it for the game's OWN log file; either way state in rationale what you accepted. Expect agentvision/log.txt (the 'text' sink) to stay permanently EMPTY for a compiled program — only the python runtime and browser ingest ever write it — so do not pin an adapter to it (the catalog's own do_not list).
recipes.visual_capture: TRUE — the gui_toolkit signal is the argument, and for a game or emulator the screen holds state no log contains: a black frame, corrupted geometry, a shader that 'succeeded'. Set capture_app to the window's app name; ASK the user for the interval and give them the trade honestly (animation and races want 0.1-0.25 s, i.e. 4-10 PNGs/second — then watch av_retention and av_frames_awaiting). Correlation rule for this shape: wrapper records always have frame_seq null (cli.py:308), unlike the python runtime which reads .av_frame_seq — so join frames and logs by TIMESTAMP via av_actions_around_frame / av_error_moment, and do not expect frame_seq matching. av_ui_tree/av_ui_diff are near-useless (an SDL/Metal window exposes no accessibility children), and OCR needs a backend installed (`agentvision install-ocr`).
recipes.what_would_still_be_invisible: A segfault or SIGKILL: you get the exit status and whatever already crossed the pipe. Output still sitting in the C stdio buffer at crash time is lost entirely — for a printf-logging program that is the single biggest blind spot, and the fix is in the target (line-buffer, or route the crash path to stderr), not in AgentVision. Anything written to a file descriptor other than stdout/stderr unless you pin that file as a log source. GPU/driver-side failure (validation-layer or Metal messages go to the system log, not your pipe). The inside of the emulator — guest registers, memory, timing — unless the program prints it. And note that av_install_verify CANNOT prove any of this works for cpp: for tee/config languages it does a STATIC check only (emitter files present + sink writable, mode='static', bridge_server.py:5816-5831), so the only real proof is a short run through `agentvision run` followed by av_log_raw. Finally, pass --no-watch-files: the wrapper's 1 s file watcher walks the whole project tree and MEASURED emits self-referential records about AgentVision's own sink (5 in a 5 s run); a game writing saves, screenshots or shader caches into the tree will flood the timeline with file events.

recipes.shape: 5. Node.js CLI tool that only prints to stdout
how_to_recognise: package.json with a "bin" entry (often "type":"module"), a bin/cli.js or src/cli.ts with a #!/usr/bin/env node shebang, commander/yargs/oclif/cac in dependencies, no server listen, frequently chalk/ora/ink/log-update.

THE DECISIVE READ IS WHICH WRITE CALL IT USES: grep for process.stdout.write versus console.log. That one fact decides whether stdout_tee means anything at all here (measured below). Spinner/ink/JSON-piping CLIs are almost always write()-based.

Also determine HOW it is launched in practice — `node dist/cli.js` versus the bin shim (`npx mytool`, `yarn mytool`) — because _child_has_inprocess_emitter keys on the literal exe name and that changes what gets captured (cli.py:352-359).

code_evidence is thin for a .ts CLI (bridge_plan._EXT_LANG has .ts but not .tsx; a compiled dist/ is skipped as 'dist'), so lean on the manifest and your own greps; async (await/Promise) is the signal most likely to fire and it is the one that matters.
recipes.why_each: stdout_tee is what turns the CLI's own output into timestamped records, and for a console.*-based CLI it genuinely works: MEASURED, `agentvision run -- node app.js` captured console.log as category=log, source=av.node.console.info. But be exact where the catalog's one-liner is broader than the code — av_emit.js patches console.log/info/warn/error/debug ONLY. In that same measured run, process.stdout.write('via-process-stdout-write') and process.stderr.write('via-process-stderr-write') produced NO record at all: the wrapper had gone mirror-only because the exe was literally 'node', and av_emit.js never touches the streams. So for a write()-based CLI this id is a promise the build does not keep, and you have two honest options: (a) keep stdout_tee but launch through a NON-node exe — MEASURED, `sh -c "node app.js"` (the same rule as npm/npx/yarn/pnpm/bin-shim) captured all three lines through the wrapper tee as av.wrapper.stdout/stderr, at the cost of duplicating console lines (av.node.console.info AND av.wrapper.stdout); or (b) select [] and say in rationale that the program 'already' prints and the wrapper tee is the bridge (validate_plan accepts an empty list only if the rationale contains 'already' or 'no log'). Optionally add uncaught_exceptions as a SECOND id if the tool is async-heavy — but only as recorded intent: av_emit.js registers uncaughtException and unhandledRejection unconditionally, and selection_report will claim enforced=true for it, which is WRONG for node (build_emitter puts AGENTVISION_HOOKS into run_env for python alone, and av_emit.js has no hooks check).
recipes.deliberately_not: browser_events — offered because the language is node, but this tool has no page; it would install no file and see nothing. logging_bridge — offered for node and implemented for nothing: av_emit.js contains no logging-framework hook at all, so pino/winston/bunyan are untouched. If the CLI uses pino, the honest move is to point pino's destination at agentvision/actions.jsonl yourself, or read its file as a log source with a verified adapter. lifecycle — av_emit.js always emits av.node.start (pid, argv, node version, cwd) and av.node.exit (code), so it is a facet you already have; spending an id on it records a build that was going to happen anyway.
recipes.adapters: Keep the structured records and pin the events label to auto/jsonl (MEASURED jsonl 1.00 on a unified record). Do NOT plan to parse the CLI's prose. Measured: 'Done in 3.2s.' is claimed by structural at 0.02 → is_fallback TRUE, which is precisely the state _validate_adapter_coverage refuses to let you seal in silence — either av_add_adapter a parser and pin it under that label, or write 'accept the weaker parse' in rationale; both are engineering answers, saying nothing is not. And 'error: could not read config: ENOENT' → frontend_build_error at 1.00 with source='build': right level, wrong source, is_fallback FALSE — a confident misparse that would scatter av_errors_by_fingerprint across a source name that is not your program. Verify with av_test_adapter on real lines from a real run before you rely on any of it.
recipes.visual_capture: FALSE. This is the SAME answer as recipe 3 and I am saying so rather than inventing a difference — a headless program has no window worth sampling. The only distinction is that a CLI is also short-lived, which makes capture doubly pointless (frames require a live window at capture time), and it makes av_wait_for/av_watch less useful too: the process is usually gone before a tripwire fires, so read the sink after the run instead.
recipes.what_would_still_be_invisible: Exit code and argv whenever the tool runs WITHOUT the wrapper: node's mechanism is env_autoload (NODE_OPTIONS=--require), there is no true autoload like python's sitecustomize, so a plain `mytool --flag` emits absolutely nothing. Everything written with process.stdout.write when launched as `node …` (measured absent). stdin — piped input is never captured, so a CLI reading a file list or JSON from a pipe has an invisible half of its input. A process.exit() mid-promise: the exit record emits, the pending async work never does. Child processes: a node child inherits NODE_OPTIONS and DOES emit into the same sink under a different run_id, but a non-node child's output is only visible if the CLI itself pipes it through. And ANSI/spinner rewriting: the terminal shows a live-updated line while the sink gets whatever discrete write calls occurred — and because the wrapper gives the child a PIPE for stdout (isatty() false), many CLIs switch to plain non-interactive output, so what you observe is not what a user sees. Confirm the emitter really loads before debugging anything else: av_install_verify actively probes node (`node -e` with NODE_OPTIONS, looking for av.node.*), which is the cheapest proof available for this shape.
